stories.Headline: 3 AI Stocks With Earnings Growth Over 33% To Watch
stories.Summary:
Meta Platforms is set to report third quarter 2026 results on Wednesday, October 21. Analysts tracked by Visible Alpha expect revenue of $63.42 billion, up 23.8 percent year over year, while capital expenditures are projected to hit $41.68 billion. That capex figure would be one of the largest single quarter infrastructure outlays ever disclosed by a consumer internet company. Meta’s new personal assistant, Muse, reportedly crossed 5 million downloads in its first 22 days, according to Sensor Tower data cited by CNBC. Analysts also estimate Meta will have used $8.52 billion in free cash flow during the quarter.

The spending plan could reach $145 billion in capital expenditures for the full year 2026, a number CNBC reported from the company’s own guidance. The free cash flow usage of $8.52 billion means Meta is expected to burn through cash rather than generate it once capital spending and operating costs are netted against incoming revenue. Reports elsewhere have floated subscription pricing tiers for Muse around $20 and $100 per month, but those specific numbers were not confirmed in the Reuters material previewing the earnings call. Claims that Muse carried an internal codename, reportedly “Hatch,” and a reported 60 percent increase in daily assistant interactions also remain unconfirmed.

Meta has spent much of 2026 defending its spending plan, and Wall Street has mostly gone along on faith that AI products would eventually generate revenue to match the outlay. The earnings call is the first real test of that faith since Muse launched widely. Meta has leaned almost entirely on a consumer assistant app, Muse, as its flagship proof point, unlike Microsoft and Google, which have leaned on enterprise cloud contracts and developer tooling. The company’s leadership became more cautious about long multi year bets after the metaverse drew heavy criticism from investors as Reality Labs losses mounted.

The next few weeks in US ad supported internet and digital advertising will be a stress test for the AI story that helped power tech through 2026. PubMatic, with all of its US$289 million in sales tied to internet information services and a market value around US$758 million, is exposed to the shift of ad budgets from traditional TV to digital channels such as connected TV, with management reporting CTV at roughly 20 percent of revenue. Sprinklr, with all US$872.9 million of revenue coming from software and programming and a stock valued at about US$1.35 billion, is benefiting from enterprise demand for AI powered analytics and automation. Viant Technology is a pure play demand side platform giving exposure to how brands buy CTV and programmatic media.

stories.Headline: AI agents targeted 1,200 websites and compromised more than 100: report
stories.Summary:
Over the past couple of weeks, a cybersecurity researcher watched a Chinese-speaking hacker break into websites belonging to more than 100 companies, including Deere, SharkNinja and Cummins. The hacker did almost none of the work directly, instead outsourcing the hacking spree almost entirely to artificial intelligence. Snorre Fagerland, principal threat researcher at the cybersecurity company NorForge, documented the activity in a report provided to Reuters ahead of publication on Monday, Oct 19. Beginning around Oct 2, Fagerland found about two dozen instances of Cairn, an open-source AI problem-solving platform popular with hackers, being used for malicious activity. This allowed him to quietly observe the cybercriminals as they set their AI tools loose on the world.

The Chinese-speaking hacker was the most prolific, beginning on Sep 25 by setting an AI army loose against US, Canadian, Australian and Japanese e-commerce websites. Their instructions were terse, sketching out preferred intrusion tactics in fewer than 100 Chinese characters. As of late last week, their agents had attempted to break into more than 1,200 sites. Successful intrusions typically took around 23 hours of probing for vulnerabilities. Fagerland estimated the campaign, which appeared to use a mixture of China's DeepSeek and Anthropic's Claude Code, had consumed roughly US$5,000 worth of tokens, or about US$50 per successful hack.

Deere told Reuters it had taken necessary remediation actions and had no indication that sensitive information was accessed. SharkNinja said the hack had hit a standalone site carrying only product support information and that the threat had been contained. Cummins said it was investigating the report of a potential cyber-attack on a website operated by one of its third-party vendors. Two smaller businesses also acknowledged being compromised, while other victims listed in the Cairn data did not return messages. Reuters could not ascertain the degree to which the breaches resulted in unauthorised extraction of data.

Fagerland said his find was real-life evidence that commercially available AI agents could pull off complex intrusions from start to finish without human intervention. He said he had previously assumed hacker-agents would need at least some supervision, but it was now obvious the technology had moved past that. Cairn's author, whose social media handle is le1xia0, said the platform was an innovative type of multi-agent architecture and was not designed for hacking attacks. In August, the Israeli firm Gambit Security found that Russian-speaking extortionists had leveraged SpaceX's Cursor AI tool to break into seven organisations. In September, Gambit documented an AI agent-driven spree that resulted in breaches at 25 companies and the theft of at least 600,000 credit card records.

stories.Headline: Nvidia-backed Nscale, Anthropic in talks for new US$45 billion AI cloud deal, source says
stories.Summary:
Nscale is in talks to sell artificial intelligence computing power to Anthropic, the maker of Claude, in a new deal that could be worth about US$45 billion, a person familiar with the matter told Reuters on Oct 19. The data centre developer is seeking another major agreement with the AI lab for a second facility at its Monarch data centre campus in West Virginia. In August, Anthropic struck a deal to spend US$45 billion to rent AI cloud computing power from Nscale’s West Virginia campus. A second Monarch building would deliver 460 megawatts of computing power using Nvidia’s advanced Vera Rubin AI chips, according to the source.

Anthropic also has the right of first refusal on Monarch’s expected third building, the person said, adding that discussions were ongoing and details of the plan could change. Anthropic did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment. Bloomberg, which first reported the news, also said a cohort of investors had urged Anthropic to lower its initial public offering valuation target after a series of market setbacks for AI companies. Investors have sharpened scrutiny of companies that are increasingly turning to debt-driven AI infrastructure expansion. Last week, Nscale rival CoreWeave’s shares slumped amid concerns over its US$50 billion debt load, fuelling a global sell-off in AI stocks.

The news of a potential tie-up comes after Microsoft pulled out of a deal to anchor a flagship data centre for Nscale following power connection delays that pushed its expected supply date into the 2030s. Nscale has grown rapidly since launch, increasing its total contracted value from US$100 million to more than US$103 billion in two-and-a-half years and competing with Nebius, Crusoe and Lambda. According to the Nscale prospectus, Microsoft and Anthropic are expected to be the company’s major customers in the future. The deal is not final and terms could still change.

stories.Headline: Oracle & AstraZeneca to link AI research with care
stories.Summary:
Oracle and AstraZeneca have agreed to explore how artificial intelligence and real world data could be used in clinical research and patient care. The companies announced the non binding agreement on 21 October 2026. The initial disease areas under consideration are oncology, cardiovascular, renal and metabolic diseases, respiratory and immunology, and rare diseases. The work would combine AstraZeneca’s scientific and therapeutic expertise with Oracle’s health data, cloud, analytics and clinical workflow tools.

The collaboration is intended to test selected use cases rather than launch a full commercial programme at this stage. The companies plan to examine how clinicians could use data and AI to identify eligible patients for clinical trials, speed up evidence generation and bring research findings into day to day care. They also plan to explore a continuous learning model in which insights from clinical research and routine care inform future study design, safety monitoring and patient care. That model would rely on shared governance, reusable technical components and agreed outcome measures to assess results. These measures would help determine whether successful approaches could be extended across disease areas and geographies.

Pascal Soriot, Chief Executive Officer of AstraZeneca, said the collaboration brings leaders in healthcare and AI together at a global scale to accelerate the journey from medicine discovery to patient care. Anne Claire Gerbaldi, Chief Digital, Data and AI Officer at AstraZeneca, said too many patients are diagnosed late or face a long journey to get the care they need. Oracle executives Sicilia and Verma said better use of data can help turn scientific innovation into better outcomes for patients, and that progress depends on shortening the distance between scientific insight and the decisions clinicians make every day. Oracle Health and Life Sciences is expected to provide the technology and data environment for the work.

The agreement reflects a broader effort across the healthcare industry to use AI and large datasets to improve the connection between medical research and clinical decision making. Drugmakers and health technology groups have been seeking ways to use routine care data more effectively, particularly in trial recruitment, evidence generation and safety monitoring. Oracle has been expanding its healthcare and life sciences work in data, cloud systems and clinical applications. AstraZeneca, one of the world’s largest pharmaceutical groups, has been investing in digital and data led approaches to drug development and patient care. Any progress will depend on governance arrangements within the health systems delivering care.

stories.Headline: What happens when good AI goes bad?
stories.Summary:
Researchers warn that artificial intelligence could turn from being helpful to doing harm, and they are working to predict when that change might happen. Neil Johnson, a professor of physics and data science at George Washington University, has been studying this tipping point. He said there is essentially zero other research on this tipping point. Johnson has been developing a formula that shows what happens when AI agents people rely on for answers begin giving suggestions that are wrong, misleading, or potentially dangerous.

The research focuses on smaller AI systems running on devices like phones, which could give bad advice to a teen or a vulnerable person. Johnson said the main concern is not AI firing missiles into the moon, but people using AI in an isolated way, because those users are susceptible to the tipping point no matter what major companies do. He is working on predicting how that tipping point can be delayed or prevented by changing prompts and training AI. The articles were published on Oct. 20, 2026, and updated about two hours before publication.

Johnson is the main researcher named in the articles, and he compared the shift in AI to the story of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde, where a scientist suddenly changes to a frightening side of his personality. He said isolation will happen as more people start using AI that is available on devices. The articles do not name any specific AI companies or products involved in the research. They also do not describe any actual harmful event that has already occurred, only the possibility that one could happen in the future.

The articles do not say what specific next steps Johnson or other researchers will take beyond continuing to study how prompts and training can delay or prevent the tipping point. They also do not mention any government regulation, new laws, or company policies that might be introduced. The reporting comes from InvestigateTV and was carried by several local stations, including fox5vegas.com, azfamily.com, and wafb.com. No timeline is given for when the research might produce practical tools or recommendations.

stories.Headline: New UN initiative will aim to tackle the military uses of AI
stories.Summary:
The United Nations is launching a new initiative on the military uses of artificial intelligence to address concerns about the threat the technology could pose to humanity. The initiative is being led by the U.N. Institute for Disarmament Research, known as UNIDIR, and it plans to launch on Thursday. It will establish the first international forum for key players to try to tackle the issue. Robin Geiss, head of the Geneva-based institute, warned at a U.N. press conference on Tuesday that the margin for human judgment is increasingly narrow, including in the nuclear domain.

Geiss said it is difficult to assess how close the world is to machines possibly acting outside of human control, and that uncertainty is the issue the initiative is trying to resolve. He noted that AI is increasingly creeping into areas such as early warning systems, information gathering, and reconnaissance, making it quite difficult to say at which point control is actually being lost. Geiss said there was widespread reluctance to deal with AI guardrails for a long time, but the proliferation of capabilities has led to a growing realization that now is the time to act on military AI. He also pointed to a proposal last month for the U.S. and China to set up an AI safety alert system for issues that could threaten national security.

UNIDIR this summer established a Center of Excellence on AI, Peace and Security, the first permanent platform by the world body focused on those issues. Geiss said it received funding from all five major nuclear powers, the U.S., Russia, China, Britain, and France. On Thursday, UNIDIR will launch a new forum as part of the center to bring together actors from every relevant sector and all over the world to work on AI in military uses. Another effort will focus on the role of industry and aims to develop a framework for responsible industry behavior.

Geiss said decisions by companies on design and development determine whether AI-enabled military capabilities are ultimately reliable, predictable, and able to operate in line with international law. For that reason, UNIDIR is developing a framework of responsible industry behavior that will provide practical, voluntary guidelines that follow international law and ensure human rights. The U.N. agency will hold consultations this week with defense technology companies, software developers, subcontractors, investors, and others alongside governments, civil society, academia, and experts. UNIDIR is also launching an initiative focused on the risks of AI misuse by armed groups, warning that such actors are already using the technology to support operational planning, execution, and logistics.

stories.Headline: Chinese AI tool behind cyberattacks in Japan: Security firm - CNA
stories.Summary:
A Chinese AI cybersecurity tool called Artex was used in a spate of recent hacks of Japanese companies, according to the information security arm of GMO Internet Group, which announced the finding on Tuesday, Oct 20. Dozens of Japanese companies, from restaurant chains to a car hire operator, have disclosed unauthorised access or data breaches in recent weeks, potentially impacting millions of customers. GMO Cybersecurity by Ierae, a subsidiary of GMO Internet Group, said it had confirmed Artex was used after investigating the attacks in collaboration with external organisations. Daiki Fukumori of GMO wrote on the company blog that the attacks were almost exclusively targeting Japan.

The GMO subsidiary discovered six internet servers launching AI-powered attacks, with each server broadly categorised by industries such as finance, e-commerce and logistics. The locations of the servers and who may have been operating them were not given. A survey released by Teikoku Databank earlier that week said around one-sixth of Japanese companies had suffered breaches. The Straits Times reported that eight firms disclosed leaked or possibly leaked data in September and October, with attacks hitting retail, logistics and financial companies. Artex was designed to help organisations strengthen their cyber defences through AI-powered security testing to find potential weak points, its developer has said.

The Chinese tool this month stopped programmers from accessing its source code, acknowledging misuse by bad actors after South Korea linked it to several hacks on financial institutions. A statement from the developer said using Artex for cyberattacks was entirely contrary to the project's intentions, adding that the project would no longer be updated. Daiki Fukumori said GMO had shared the information with law enforcement agencies to prevent further damage. Toshiharu Furukawa, Japan's minister in charge of cybersecurity, said at a press conference on Oct 20 that the government was analysing whether there was malicious use of AI after hearing from companies that sustained damage, and vowed to continue efforts to prevent cyberattacks.

The Japanese government has called on companies to strengthen their cyber defences, and this month the head of the ruling party's cybersecurity committee said a state of emergency had been reached over emerging threats. The attacks on Japanese companies may be similar to those on South Korean financial organisations that CrowdStrike, a US cybersecurity firm, reported earlier in October, as both involved Artex. A separate investigation indicated Artex involvement in a series of unauthorised accesses to South Korean financial institutions since late September. The articles did not specify further steps beyond the government's ongoing analysis and its pledge to keep working to stop attacks.

stories.Headline: 3 Artificial Intelligence (AI) Stocks That Look Like Great Buys Right Now
stories.Summary:
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing, or TSMC, reported its third quarter earnings on October 19, 2026, showing strong growth. The company generated $46.7 billion in revenue, a 41 percent increase year over year. It also posted a gross margin of 66.4 percent and an operating margin of 58.7 percent. Management expects revenue between $52.3 billion and $54.3 billion for the fourth quarter as its 2-nanometer technology ramps up.

The article argues TSMC has more upside through 2030 than Nvidia or Micron. Nvidia faces competition from custom chips made by Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft, and Meta Platforms, while Micron faces a cyclical memory market and competition from China's ChangXin Memory Technologies. TSMC, by contrast, can manufacture chips for many different companies regardless of which designs win. Building a foundry requires large upfront capital and years of engineering, creating high barriers to entry. As AI workloads shift from training large language models toward inference in autonomous systems and robotics, TSMC should benefit from broader demand.

Adam Spatacco of The Motley Fool wrote the analysis. He said TSMC does not need Nvidia to beat Alphabet's custom chip strategy because it can make chips for both companies. He also said TSMC's versatility could support more valuation expansion than other semiconductor stocks. He described TSMC as a compelling buy-and-hold AI chip stock through 2030.

The context is that investors are trying to identify which chipmakers will dominate in five years. Nvidia remains the leader in AI accelerators thanks to its GPUs and CUDA software, but its largest customers are developing alternatives. Micron's memory products are essential for AI computing, but expanded production could pressure prices by next decade. TSMC's stock traded at $420.22 on October 19, 2026, with a market cap of $2.18 trillion. The article does not say what happens next beyond the fourth quarter revenue projection.

stories.Headline: S. Korea's U.N. envoy named co-chair of global AI governance dialogue - Yonhap News Agency
stories.Summary:
South Korea's ambassador to the United Nations, Cha Ji-hoon, has been appointed as co-chair of a U.N. initiative on artificial intelligence governance. The appointment was made by the president of the U.N. General Assembly on Friday, according to the U.N. website on Tuesday. He will serve alongside Mutryce Agatha Williams, the permanent representative of Saint Kitts and Nevis. Together they will lead preparations for the 2027 Global Dialogue on AI Governance.

The dialogue is scheduled for May 3-4, 2027, and will bring together governments and other stakeholders to discuss international cooperation on AI governance. The initiative was established under a U.N. General Assembly resolution adopted in August 2025. It serves as a platform for discussions involving governments, the private sector, civil society and researchers. South Korea is expected to play a coordinating role in preparations for the next round of international discussions on AI governance.

The country seeks to become one of the world's top three AI powerhouses under the current Lee Jae Myung administration. Separately, Choi Ji-young, executive director of the IMF Asia and the Pacific Constituency Office, said in Bangkok on Thursday that South Korea appears to be weathering global economic headwinds thanks to the AI boom. He cited trade tensions, the Middle East crisis and the war between Russia and Ukraine as lingering sources of uncertainty. The IMF raised its growth forecast for South Korea in 2026 to 3.3 percent, up 0.7 percentage point from its July projection, citing strong semiconductor exports driven by AI infrastructure demand.

Choi said AI-related investment will likely continue for some time, noting that building AI data centers takes a long time, potentially around 10 years. He said investment has only just begun and these projects are unlikely to falter in a couple of years. He added that the IMF sees potential downsides in AI, including a stock market correction, an adjustment in the current account and adverse effects on businesses should the AI boom falter. However, within the organization, the expectation is that AI investment will continue for a long time. Choi also noted the AI boom has expanded South Korea's fiscal room to invest more in future growth, and he advised countries experiencing economic growth to prioritize investment in innovation and growth rather than focusing excessively on debt-to-GDP ratios.

stories.Headline: Rogers, El-Sayed outline differing approaches to tariffs and AI during Detroit Economic Club forum
stories.Summary:
U.S. Senate nominees Mike Rogers and Abdul El-Sayed appeared separately at a Detroit Economic Club forum on Tuesday, Oct. 20, with the Nov. 3 election two weeks away. Both agreed that tariffs could be useful economic tools if applied carefully, and both said artificial intelligence needs federal guardrails. Rogers said President Trump’s tariffs helped bring manufacturing back to the United States, but he criticized the tariff war with Canada as unhelpful to the automotive industry. El-Sayed said he was not against tariffs in general, only what he called dumb tariffs, and he argued that Trump’s version has been terrible for American auto workers.

El-Sayed proposed building a $25,000 electric vehicle with a 300-mile range over the next seven years, using subsidies for the first two years and tariffs on the EV market to compete with Chinese low-cost EVs. Rogers said General Motors is bringing about 500,000 new cars to be built in the United States, including Silverados at the Orion plant, and that Detroit Diesel was adding a third shift because of tariff policies. On education, Rogers said two-thirds of fourth graders in Detroit cannot read at grade level, and that in eighth grade only 15% of Detroit students read at grade level while only 12% can do math at grade level. El-Sayed said he supports a Medicare-for-All system, while Rogers advocated for price transparency in health care.

Rogers said he supports a national security framework for AI and may back a narrowly crafted antitrust exemption so AI companies can share safety information. He recalled being briefed before leaving Congress in 2014 on an early AI-guided missile that appeared to make its own decisions during a test. El-Sayed said the CEOs of OpenAI and Anthropic agree that AI could take 50% of white collar jobs in America over a five to 10 year time horizon, not 25 to 50 years. He called for an SEC or FDA-style regulatory agency to oversee AI development, and said AI should not be able to fire weapons, fire people, or deny health care.

The race is rated a tossup by the Cook Political Report. The forum was hosted by WDIV-TV anchor Jason Colthorp at the Masonic, and the candidates answered the same questions separately without mentioning each other by name. They were set to debate again on Wednesday evening. Rogers said it is better to send someone to Washington who can negotiate with Trump on tariffs, while El-Sayed said Rogers supported NAFTA as a congressman and that it hemorrhaged jobs in Michigan. El-Sayed also said legacy AI corporations should be rebuilt as public interest corporations, with democratically appointed leadership of at least 50% of their boards and the government holding about 50% of the value.

stories.Headline: OpenAI seeks to accelerate fundraising ahead of Anthropic IPO, sources say
stories.Summary:
OpenAI is racing to secure investor commitments before rival Anthropic’s expected public market debut in mid-November, according to two sources familiar with the matter. The unusually fast fundraising could value the ChatGPT maker at more than US$1.4 trillion. SoftBank Group, Abu Dhabi-based MGX and other existing backers are in talks to join the round of about US$30 billion. OpenAI held meetings with long-only funds and sovereign wealth funds last week while Anthropic was hosting its own investor day. The rapid timetable reflects a desire to get ahead of Anthropic as the two frontier labs increasingly tap a similar investor base.

OpenAI is pitching investors on growth that accelerated after the launch of its GPT-6 Astra model, saying it had reached US$50 billion in annualised revenue and expecting that figure to rise to US$70 billion by the end of 2026. Anthropic’s annualised revenue reached roughly US$65 billion by July, and its quarterly revenue jumped to US$16.8 billion in the third quarter from US$11.6 billion in the second quarter of 2026. OpenAI records revenue on a net basis by subtracting partner shares upfront, and it has accused Anthropic of inflating its revenue by counting the full, gross value of contracts sold through third-party cloud providers. OpenAI was last valued at US$852 billion in March, after a record-breaking US$122 billion funding round, including a commitment from Amazon.com, which agreed to invest up to US$50 billion.

OpenAI and SoftBank declined to comment, while Anthropic and MGX did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Edward Best, co-chair of capital markets at Willkie Farr & Gallagher, who is not working on the deal and commented on a hypothetical basis, said OpenAI could want to set its own valuation and not have to worry about a comparison. He added that it is really a two-horse race in terms of being public. Some investors view OpenAI’s financing push as an effort to lock in capital from funds that might otherwise devote more of their resources to Anthropic’s IPO.

A number of companies preparing to go public have decided to wait until after Anthropic’s planned IPO, wary of competing for investor demand amid market volatility and a pullback in AI stocks. Some existing and prospective Anthropic investors have argued for a valuation closer to US$1.5 trillion for its market debut, instead of the desired US$2 trillion, after the AI start-up’s third-quarter results fell short of expectations. The uncertainty has disrupted what had been expected to be a busy autumn for IPOs, with companies reassessing their listing plans. Blackstone-backed AirTrunk REIT, Nvidia-backed Firmus and SoftBank-backed SB Energy have either pulled or paused their listings. Nuclear services company Holtec cited a “perfect storm”, driven mainly by uncertainty around data centre demand, when it pulled its US listing in September.

stories.Headline: China moves to tighten AI export controls amid US rivalry
stories.Summary:
China has proposed export controls on 23 artificial intelligence technologies, including those involving models, agents and computing clusters. The proposal was announced by China’s Commerce Ministry on 20 October 2026 in Beijing. It is intended to tighten oversight of technology that China considers important to national security and geopolitical competition with Washington. The controls would cover overseas deployment of AI models containing restricted technology but exclude access through application programming interfaces, websites, apps and software-as-a-service platforms.

The proposals form part of a broader revision of China’s technology export catalogue covering 40 technologies across AI, biotechnology and solar power. They also include prohibiting transfers of intellectual property ownership involving some novel cell and gene therapies and small interfering RNA technologies. Most AI technologies would remain freely exportable, with simplified licensing for open-source technology exports and Chinese companies operating their own computing centers overseas. Technology already in the public domain through open-source releases or academic papers would also fall outside the proposed controls.

Exporters must register certain overseas technology transfers from 30 October, pending final rules after public consultation closes on 15 November. The Commerce Ministry said the proposed controls were partly intended to prevent the misuse of AI technologies, including systems capable of autonomously generating and modifying malicious software that could threaten critical infrastructure and national security. The distinction in the rules could allow Chinese AI developers such as DeepSeek and Alibaba to continue expanding internationally while giving Beijing greater oversight of transfers of sensitive AI technology abroad. Reuters reported in July that Chinese authorities had discussed potentially restricting overseas access to China’s most advanced AI models, including unreleased ones, with major technology companies including Alibaba, ByteDance and Z.AI.

The measures come as China and the United States compete for leadership in AI. Washington’s restrictions on China’s access to cutting-edge American AI chips have helped keep U.S. firms Anthropic and OpenAI in the lead, although Chinese rivals are finding workarounds to narrow the gap. Chinese AI models have gained ground overseas because of lower prices and improving capabilities since DeepSeek’s R1 model emerged early last year. At the same time, the two countries have agreed to keep humans in control of nuclear-weapons decisions and last month established a dialogue and incident-communications channel for advanced AI.

stories.Headline: Boeing Teams Up With Microsoft To Build New AI-Powered Dataliner Platform – BMO Sees ‘Upside Tension’ For Azure
stories.Summary:
Boeing announced Dataliner on Tuesday, an AI-powered data intelligence platform developed with Microsoft to help airlines improve fleet-wide maintenance and operational decisions. The platform combines aviation data, AI, and Boeing’s aircraft and engineering expertise to give airlines a more complete view of their fleets, including aircraft condition, maintenance history, and operations. Boeing said Dataliner will give airlines broader insights into aircraft condition, maintenance history, and fleet operations. Boeing and Microsoft shares traded marginally lower at the time of the announcement. Dataliner uses Azure AI Foundry, Microsoft’s data solutions, and other technologies, and it allows airlines to keep data in their own environments and choose what information they share.

Airlines can access Boeing and industry intelligence through applications, APIs, analytics, and AI-enabled experiences. Boeing said the platform includes access controls, encryption, and monitoring to help protect sensitive aviation data, and its on-demand sharing model does not require airlines to centralize their data on a single platform. Boeing plans to use Dataliner to support new digital services, including Asset Lifecycle Planning and TechOps AI Agent, while connecting existing offerings such as Airplane Health Management, Insight Accelerator, and Maintenance Performance Toolbox. Lindsey Douglas, vice president of Cabin, Modifications, Maintenance and Digital Services at Boeing Global Services, said Dataliner is an important step in bringing Boeing’s aircraft expertise and digital capabilities together to help customers anticipate maintenance needs, identify emerging risks, and take timely action. Chris Barry, president of U.S. Public Sector Industries at Microsoft, said the platform gives airlines a secure, scalable foundation to turn fragmented data into fleet-wide intelligence by combining Boeing’s OEM and aviation expertise with Microsoft’s trusted data and AI technologies.

Separately, BMO Capital raised its price target on Microsoft to $600 from $515 while maintaining an Outperform rating, according to The Fly. BMO sees upside tension to its first quarter Azure revenue estimates, citing positive cloud-check feedback, and believes Azure revenue can accelerate in the first quarter compared with the first quarter. For Microsoft 365, BMO said the company’s shift toward a consumption-based model could support average revenue per user and sales mix as seat growth moderates. Retail sentiment on Stocktwits for Boeing remained in bearish territory over the past 24 hours with extremely high message volume, while sentiment around Microsoft continued to trend in the extremely bearish zone with normal levels of chatter. Microsoft shares have gained over 9 percent year-to-date, whereas Boeing shares have dropped over 11 percent year-to-date.

stories.Headline: Microsoft Adds Guardian Agents to Treat Enterprise AI Agents as Potential Insider Threats
stories.Summary:
Microsoft introduced new security features on 20 October 2026 aimed at protecting enterprises from risks posed by AI agents, headlined by a tool called Guardian Agents. The announcement came from Hayete Gallot, executive vice president of Microsoft Security, who outlined how the company plans to monitor, manage and contain what it calls agentic insiders. These are AI agents deployed within a company that can access data, use software tools and make decisions without constant human supervision. The new focus is part of Project Perception, which Microsoft first introduced in June with red, blue and green teams of agents to attack, detect and fix vulnerabilities from outside threats.

The changes require enterprises to treat AI agents as potential insider threats, even when those agents have not been compromised by an attacker. Microsoft has added agent detection to Microsoft Defender, identifying up to 60 agent types including Claude Code and Codex. The new controls limit agent access, adjust permissions by task and require human approval for risky actions. Guardian Agents are specialized AI agents that supervise other agents and step in when their behavior gets risky, which might mean limiting an agent's permissions or blocking certain actions before they cause harm. Gallot said frontier models cannot be trusted regardless of origin, not because they are malicious but because they are unpredictable, trained to complete tasks rather than follow organizational norms, and often granted broad access to sensitive data and tools.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella argued in an October 10 essay that enterprises should stop relying on AI model providers' safety assurances and instead use independent systems to oversee agents. He wrote that enterprises should treat powerful AI models much like potential insider security risks, particularly when those models can access confidential information or perform critical business operations. Nadella called for security controls that operate independently of AI models, including restricted permissions, detailed activity logging and mechanisms that allow administrators to stop an agent's actions. He said the supply of intelligence should be separated from the authority over it.

Project Perception was first introduced in July and entered public preview on August 3, designed to help security teams respond to increasingly sophisticated cyberthreats using AI-powered automation. The system pulls in security data from identities, endpoints, cloud environments, applications and other sources to spot threats and respond faster. Gallot said monitoring and securing agents must become continuous, and future security tools will also need to show why AI models make the choices they do, not just what actions they end up taking. Microsoft is also an inaugural member of Nvidia's Open Agent Safety Platform, and the stance is notable given Microsoft's investments in both OpenAI and Anthropic.

stories.Headline: Chinese teen AI prodigy Nathan Chen said to be joining US start-up Discovery Loop
stories.Summary:
Nathan Chen Guangyu, a 17 year old Chinese AI researcher, is reported to be joining Discovery Loop, a US AI start-up, just days after announcing his departure from Moonshot AI. The news was posted on Tuesday by Arfur Grok, a widely watched anonymous social media account that tracks AI talent movements in the US. Discovery Loop was founded by four former Google senior researchers, including former chief scientist Jeff Dean. Chen did not immediately respond to a request for comment, and Discovery Loop said it does not comment on personnel matters.

Discovery Loop was launched just two months ago and has already recruited several star researchers from US big tech giants, including other former Google engineers. Its initial funding round was led by Radical Ventures and Khosla Ventures, with Google parent Alphabet also an investor. Business Insider reported last month that the start-up was seeking a valuation of around $50 billion in another funding round. At the Agentic AI Summit at the University of California, Berkeley, in early August, Jeff Dean described a vision in which AI could run thousands of scientific experiments in parallel and use their results to select subsequent experiments. He said this could shorten the scientific process from years to hours or even minutes.

Moonshot senior researcher Du Yulun wrote in a social media post that he and Chen had several long conversations about his decision to leave. Du said it was ultimately best for Chen to explore and follow his new curiosity as much as possible at his age. During his time at Moonshot, which lasted less than a year, Chen helped pioneer technical breakthroughs that delivered cost efficiency gains for its flagship Kimi models. These gains made the models competitive with US heavyweights such as OpenAI’s GPT and Anthropic’s Claude.

Discovery Loop has yet to release any products, but its mission is to automate scientific research with AI. Chen is likely to be one of its youngest members at just 17 years old. The start-up’s work would be similar to efforts to achieve recursive self improvement, the stated goal of leading AI companies in both the US and China. No further confirmation of Chen’s hiring had been provided by either Chen or Discovery Loop at the time of the reports.

stories.Headline: Meta Platforms (META) Q3 earnings preview: Can AI returns justify surging infrastructure spending?
stories.Summary:
Meta Platforms is scheduled to report its third quarter 2026 results after the US market closes on Wednesday, 21 October 2026, followed by an earnings call at 4:30 pm Eastern Time. The company faces a critical test of whether its artificial intelligence investments are generating enough returns to justify surging infrastructure spending. Meta’s shares fell 2.82 percent from the start of October through 19 October 2026, while several Magnificent Seven peers rose over the same period. Investors are increasingly questioning whether rising capital expenditure will translate into sustainable earnings growth.

The street expects Meta’s third quarter revenue to rise 23.6 percent year on year to 63.34 billion US dollars, near the upper end of management’s guidance range of 61 billion to 64 billion dollars. Third quarter earnings per share are expected to come in at 6.53 dollars, and options markets are pricing in roughly a 7.1 percent earnings move, below Meta’s ten year average peak earnings day move of 10.4 percent. Meta’s full year 2026 capital expenditure guidance is 130 billion to 145 billion dollars, including finance lease principal payments, after the lower end was raised from 125 billion dollars in July. Full year 2026 operating expenses are guided at 165 billion to 169 billion dollars, reflecting higher infrastructure costs, AI related research and development, and legal expenses.

Kelvin Wong, a senior market analyst at OANDA, wrote that advertising remains Meta’s core earnings engine, but investors increasingly want evidence that AI tools can lift monetisation and justify rapidly rising infrastructure spending. He said capex, margins and free cash flow are the key risks, especially if management signals another sizeable increase in AI related spending heading into 2027. Wong also noted that Meta’s Muse AI assistant has attracted more than two million daily users, although demonstrating meaningful revenue conversion remains a key challenge. He added that management previously indicated full year 2026 operating income should exceed 2025 levels.

Technically, Wong identified 653.17 as the key medium term support, also the 50 day moving average, while a break above 734.84 may reopen the path towards 777.60 and 793.70. A daily close below 653.17 would negate the bullish tone and suggest a potential slide towards the 200 day moving average at 626.68, with major support at 540.90 below that. The most bullish outcome would combine stronger advertising revenue, resilient operating margins and convincing evidence that AI adoption is translating into higher monetisation, without another substantial increase in projected expenditure. Conversely, even an earnings beat may fail to support the share if management signals accelerating AI costs, weaker free cash flow or limited revenue visibility into 2027.

stories.Headline: FastMetal launches Google's frontier model 'Gemini 4 Argon'
stories.Summary:
FastMetal, operated by Kokusai Chotatsu Joho Co., Ltd. in Tokyo, began offering Google's large language model Gemini 4 Argon on October 14, 2026. Google had announced the model on September 30, 2026. FastMetal charges 357.4 yen per million input tokens and 1,787 yen per million output tokens, before tax, in Japanese yen with prepayment. The service works from the FastMetal web chat screen on the day of registration, and the company confirmed before launch that requests including images and PDFs returned correct responses and billing.

The model handles about one million tokens at a time, with FastMetal providing a context length of 1,048,576 tokens. It can read text, images, and PDFs. Google reported scores of 77.9 percent on DeepSWE v1.1 for software development and 91.7 percent on LVBench for long video understanding. Google's API pricing starts at US$2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with rates set to double after November 30. FastMetal says Google described this as an introductory price, and FastMetal will revise its own price when Google's changes.

Kokusai Chotatsu Joho, led by representative director Darshan Nadeau, said the yen based prepaid system avoids unexpected charges beyond the loaded balance. Payment is possible by credit card or bank transfer, and the company issues qualified invoices under Japan's invoice system with registration number T5010001015990. Google said the model is designed for deep work across coding, finance, law, cybersecurity, and science. Google also said teams using Argon in its Antigravity coding tool increased agentic code submissions by more than 35 percent while reducing code rollbacks by nearly a third.

The launch followed delays and a leadership change at Google's DeepMind lab. In September, Google said it no longer planned to release Gemini 3.5 Pro, which CEO Sundar Pichai had earlier said would arrive in June. DeepMind co-founder and CEO Demis Hassabis stepped aside, and several Gemini model leaders left. Early customers testing Argon include Deloitte, LexisNexis, Ambience Healthcare, and Isomorphic Labs. Google will expand its Fairwind Program to hundreds of additional partners, giving vetted cybersecurity defenders a version of Argon without cyber guardrails, and will give 10,000 scientists six months of free access to Antigravity's highest usage tier.

stories.Headline: Hanmi Semiconductor Opens Silicon Valley Unit to Serve U.S. Chip Plants - Seoul Economic Daily
stories.Summary:
Hanmi Semiconductor opened a new U.S. subsidiary, Hanmi USA, in San Jose, California, on October 16, with an opening ceremony attended by Chairman Kwak Dong-shin and other senior executives. The company announced the move on October 19, saying it aims to expand equipment supply opportunities and strengthen technical support for local customers. This comes as major chipmakers such as SK hynix, Micron Technology, and Amkor Technology are building or expanding production facilities in the United States. Hanmi Semiconductor now has local units in the United States, Taiwan, China, and Singapore, extending its global sales and support network.

The new Silicon Valley unit is meant to respond to the buildup of U.S. chip production bases. SK hynix broke ground in August on a $4 billion high-bandwidth memory packaging plant in West Lafayette, Indiana, scheduled to begin operations in the second half of 2028. Micron is building DRAM and HBM production facilities in Idaho and pursuing a $100 billion chip plant in New York state. Amkor Technology is investing $12 billion to build a production facility in Arizona. Hanmi Semiconductor plans to station experienced engineers locally and shorten response times by setting up a base close to customers, since performance optimization and maintenance remain critical after chip equipment is installed.

Chairman Kwak Dong-shin said the United States is an important market that leads the global AI industry and advanced chip technology. He added that the company will strengthen its competitiveness by expanding close technical support for local customers and cooperation with global chipmakers. Hanmi Semiconductor is the world's largest supplier of thermal compression bonders, the key equipment used to stack and bond DRAM chips vertically for HBM. It has recently broadened its business to include 2.5D bonders for advanced packaging, which link multiple chips, and MSVP equipment that precisely cuts and inspects chip packages. The company intends to align its local support with the startup schedules of the new U.S. plants.

stories.Headline: [PRNewswire] Binance Launches Binance AI Pro - Yonhap News Agency
stories.Summary:
Binance launched Binance AI Pro on October 20, 2026, from Abu Dhabi, UAE. The finance-focused AI agent turns plain-language trading ideas into tested, automated strategies through conversation. It is available on the Binance website and app with no separate sign-up required. Users describe assets, conditions, parameters, and risk limits in ordinary language, and the tool helps fill gaps, improves the strategy, and renders it as a visual workflow for review.

The tool generates each strategy as a visual workflow called the Strategy Canvas, shown alongside the chat on desktop, while mobile building and refining happen through chat. Workflows extend beyond trading to daily reports, market monitoring, subscription alerts, and signal generation. Every strategy can be tested with paper trading using virtual funds before any live deployment. Going live requires a separate review-and-approve step and runs in a dedicated AI Strategy Account, a virtual sub-account isolated from the user's main Binance account. Only the user can fund it through manual transfer, the agent cannot move funds by itself, and strategies can be paused, adjusted, or revoked at any time.

Jeff Li, VP of Product at Binance, said Binance AI Pro is about access, professional-style strategy building with no coding required and the user in control at every step. He said users describe the idea, review the workflow, test it with paper trading, and approve deployment themselves. The design follows bounded autonomy principles from a policy paper published earlier in October 2026 by Binance's Global Policy team, meaning agents analyze and recommend but consequential actions always require explicit human approval. Binance AI Pro supports Spot and USDS-M Futures strategies, with full availability subject to regional restrictions.

All users start on the free Standard Plan, which includes 250,000 monthly credits. The Premium Plan costs 19.99 USDC per month, raises the allowance to 10 million monthly credits, adds frontier models such as ChatGPT Sol, ChatGPT Astra, and Claude Opus where available, and allows credit top-ups. Up to 10 strategies per user are allowed across paper trading, live trading, and signals. Backtesting is not available in the initial release, and strategy sub-accounts cannot withdraw to external addresses. Binance AI Pro will progressively add support for more trading and exchange products.

stories.Headline: WELL Health Strengthens Privacy and AI Governance Leadership with Appointment of Samara Starkman as Chief Privacy Officer and Vice President, Legal & Regulatory
stories.Summary:
WELL Health Technologies Corp. appointed Samara Starkman as Chief Privacy Officer and Vice President, Legal & Regulatory, effective immediately, on October 20, 2026. Ms. Starkman previously led the privacy department at Cancer Care Ontario, now part of Ontario Health, and co-founded INQ Consulting while serving as a Partner at INQ Law. She has advised major Ontario hospitals, pharmaceutical and health-tech companies on privacy, compliance, health law, data governance and technology matters. She holds a Juris Doctor and a Master of Laws, and is a Certified Information Privacy Professional/Canada, a Certified Information Privacy Manager and a Fellow of Information Privacy.

Her mandate includes building and maturing a scalable, enterprise-wide privacy program across WELL Health, WELLSTAR and HEALWELL AI. She will lead AI governance and provide healthcare regulatory leadership as WELL's businesses navigate Canada's increasingly complex regulatory environment. Ms. Starkman will work closely with functional and business teams to embed privacy and regulatory considerations into operations, technology, products and growth initiatives. WELL owns and operates 275 clinics in Canada, supporting more than 5 million annual patient visits.

Hamed Shahbazi, Founder, Chairman and CEO of WELL, said that as WELL scales AI across its clinics, WELLSTAR and HEALWELL AI, privacy and governance must keep pace with innovation. He said Ms. Starkman's appointment gives WELL a dedicated leader with deep healthcare privacy and regulatory expertise to build that foundation enterprise-wide. Loreto Grimaldi, Chief Legal Officer of WELL, added that a key priority has been building a Law Department with the depth to support the full mandate of legal, compliance, governance, privacy, regulatory affairs and enterprise risk. Ms. Starkman said she looks forward to building an enterprise-wide privacy program and leading the development of an AI governance framework to ensure WELL's AI systems are developed and deployed safely, ethically, transparently and responsibly.

The appointment comes as Canadian healthcare legal leaders discuss AI governance, cybersecurity and privacy law reform. At a Canadian Lawyer Leaders Network roundtable, senior in-house counsel from Trillium Health Partners, Organon Canada, Edwards Lifesciences, Medcan and dentalcorp Health Services Ltd. shared views on AI tools and governance frameworks. Nicole Vaz of Trillium Health Partners said the most significant issue is establishing a governance framework that enables quick deployment while allowing monitoring, modification and redeployment. Luciana Andrade of Edwards Lifesciences noted that Canadian subsidiaries can be excluded from global AI tool deployments, causing delays in access.

stories.Headline: Anthropic posts $80bn loss in first half of 2026: WSJ
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the artificial intelligence company behind the Claude chatbot, recorded a net loss of more than $80 billion in the first half of 2026, according to a Wall Street Journal report citing its draft IPO prospectus. The loss was up from $13 billion a year earlier and was driven mainly by $72 billion in accounting charges tied to changes in the value of convertible notes and other financial instruments used to raise funding. The company also signaled it could spend up to $750 billion in coming years to acquire more computing capacity, including potential deals under discussion. Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment.

The company’s revenue jumped to $16.3 billion in the six months ended June 30, up from $1.1 billion a year earlier, while AI infrastructure spending nearly quadrupled to almost $9 billion. Anthropic told investors at a meeting that its third quarter revenue rose 45 percent to $16.8 billion from the previous quarter, and that it was profitable on an adjusted basis during that period. Some current and prospective investors who attended the investor day in San Francisco discussed a valuation of around $1.5 trillion, down from the roughly $2 trillion previously expected for the November share sale. Anthropic had pushed back its planned IPO from this month to November while still seeking to raise $100 billion.

Anthropic said Sunday it would put 5 percent of its shares into a new Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, pending stockholder approval. The fund will be a company owned limited liability corporation rather than a conventional nonprofit, and the company said none of the money would be used for lobbying or political donations. Counting earlier pledges by founders and employees, Anthropic said about a fifth of its stock will be directed to public benefit, with more possible if valuation targets are hit. SpaceX Chief Executive Elon Musk responded on X, saying he plans to hand over a share of SpaceX stock to every child in America next year, a pledge worth close to $11 billion based on about 73 million children and SpaceX closing at $147.96 Monday.

The pledges come amid rising public concern about AI’s effects on jobs. A June Pew Research Center survey found 71 percent of U.S. adults expect AI to mean fewer jobs over the next two decades, up from 64 percent in 2024. Last month, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for the industry to slow down, and OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Musk and other tech leaders expressed similar opinions. Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned in September, publicly warning about the dangers of unchecked AI development. Anthropic has already set aside $200 million to study AI’s effect on workers, and said the scale of the technology’s progress may call for bolder approaches.

stories.Headline: Personal AI Agents Including Meta’s Muse Identify Themselves Less Than 3% of Time While Handling Sensitive Transactions at Scale
stories.Summary:
Meta unveiled Muse, a personal AI assistant, on October 19, 2026, and it is now rolling out across the United States. The assistant appears in Facebook feeds with a round, rosy-cheeked mascot named Jolly. Meta describes Muse as less like a search box and more like a personal assistant that users can message with requests. It then makes a plan and carries out the work using its own secure cloud computer and browser. For example, Muse can turn a saved Instagram recipe reel into a grocery list or a dinner party plan.

The assistant can handle tasks such as selling a car, lowering a bill, or planning a trip, and it checks back when it needs approval. Meta says Muse does not share conversations or data with its ad systems, and users can opt out of having chats used to train its AI. Users can also tell Muse to forget specific details. Muse never sees passwords or card numbers, and purchases use a one-time card number with buyer protections. A separate watchdog program must approve anything Muse sends to the internet.

Meta says Muse is free for most everyday tasks, and it faces competition from ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Siri, Copilot, and Claude. The company has not said how many people are using Muse or how often it identifies itself as an AI during sensitive transactions. The articles do not say who is responsible for the low identification rate or what changes might be made next. No further rollout dates or policy updates were given.

stories.Headline: Dow Jones Futures: AMD, Nvidia Lead AI Trade Higher; Meta, Netflix, SpaceX, Tesla Earnings On Deck
stories.Summary:
SpaceX and Tesla have begun formal discussions about a possible merger, Elon Musk confirmed on October 21, 2026. Committees of independent directors at both companies were formed at shareholders’ request, and Musk said he is not taking part because of his conflict of interest. A person familiar with the matter said the talks began in recent weeks and could result in SpaceX acquiring Tesla, with Tesla working with an investment bank for advice. Musk called a combination “a good idea,” pointing to shared work in AI software, chip design, robotics and connectivity, but he cautioned that no agreement has been reached.

SpaceX reported third quarter revenue of $14.58 billion, up 161 percent from a year earlier, and net income of $4.4 billion, reversing a loss of $1.1 billion. AI revenue surged nearly tenfold to $7.56 billion, largely from renting computing capacity to developers including Anthropic, Alphabet and Reflection AI. Capital expenditure nearly tripled to $19.6 billion, and Chief Financial Officer Bret Johnsen said fourth quarter spending is expected to be between $35 billion and $40 billion. Starlink had 13.6 million subscribers, above the forecast of 12.19 million, while monthly revenue per subscriber fell to $69 from $99 in 2023. Musk also said the Terafab chip venture is expected to produce its first test chip around May or June next year, with volume production targeted for the third quarter of 2028.

Barclays suggested last week that a merger announcement could come before Tesla’s annual meeting on December 3. In an all stock deal, Barclays estimates Musk would hold about 37 percent of the equity and 56 percent of the votes. Shawn Campbell, an adviser at Camelthorn Investments, said investors are focused on Starlink revenue growth and improvement in Tesla’s auto margins. Bill Birmingham, head of research at REX Financial, said Tesla’s unveiling of a new Roadster with rocket technology on Thursday was a subtle argument for a merger ahead of the shareholder meeting.

Tesla is expected to report adjusted earnings of roughly 43 cents a share on revenue of about $27.88 billion, compared with 50 cents a year earlier. Tesla delivered 486,532 vehicles in the third quarter, beating estimates, and has said capital spending will exceed $25 billion this year. Analysts expect negative free cash flow of $4.92 billion for the third quarter. SpaceX reports results on Tuesday and Tesla on Wednesday after markets close. Evercore ISI expects SpaceX to exit 2026 at an annualized revenue run rate of about $104 billion, with capital spending reaching about $151 billion in 2027.

stories.Headline: Spotify “AI ‘one-click music’ expelled…50 million tracks removed from recommendations“
stories.Summary:
Spotify has removed more than 50 million tracks that appear to have been created by artificial intelligence from its curated music recommendations so far this year. The company announced the step on Tuesday, October 20, 2026, in a blog statement and progress report. Spotify described the mass-produced, low-quality AI music as “slop” and spam, and said such content does not belong in user recommendations. The tracks remain available on the platform but are excluded from personalized recommendation lists.

The company analyzed patterns in songs that users frequently skipped or ignored over the past six months. Those tracks consistently overlapped with artificially generated audio, which helped Spotify update its internal recommendation system. Spotify combined listener feedback with metadata and third-party AI-detection tools to limit how often AI-generated content is surfaced. Last year, the company removed 75 million tracks for serious or repeated violations of its rules, which prohibit replicating an existing creator’s content or creating media artificially with technology. To be eligible for royalties on Spotify, an artist must reach a minimum of 1,000 streams per year.

Spotify said it has improved its systems to filter out AI-generated slop and protect the listening experience. The company acknowledged that AI-detection technology has limitations and that identifying suspicious content could become more difficult as generative AI evolves. Spotify also said bad actors adapt quickly, but it believes listeners will value human artistry even more as AI makes music more abundant. Morgan Hayduk, CEO of Beatdapp, said that if the total number of streams grows because of AI slop, the percentage each legitimate rights holder or artist receives is diminished.

Spotify has introduced several features this year to increase transparency around AI use. It labels artist profiles it believes are AI-generated with an “AI Persona” badge, and those artists are excluded from user recommendation streams by default. The company also launched an AI credits feature that artists can use to disclose which parts of a song’s creative process involved AI. Spotify said these efforts have resulted in a marked decrease in listener concerns about AI spam appearing in recommendations. More than 300,000 artists, representing more than 99 percent of what listeners search for on Spotify, are now verified.

stories.Headline: DeepSeek Open-Sources DeepInfer, the Inference Framework Behind DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash
stories.Summary:
DeepSeek open-sourced DeepInfer on October 20, 2026, the inference framework that runs its production services and powers the DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash model. The company released the code under the Apache 2.0 license, and it also published deepseek-recipe, an MIT-licensed token encoding and decoding layer. DeepInfer was originally built primarily on vLLM, with ideas taken from SGLang and TensorRT-LLM. The release covers offline inference with the core features needed for serving at scale.

The framework supports one model, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, with a 1 million token context window according to the model card. It runs on NVIDIA SM100 Blackwell GPUs and Huawei Ascend 950 NPUs, with benchmarks using 4 GPUs for prefill and 64 for decode. DeepSeek reports that a single cluster serves 155 trillion tokens per day and earns US$38 per GPU-hour at valley pricing. The best decode performance is above 25,000 output tokens per second per GPU at 256 requests per rank, while prefill reaches about 60,000 non-cached tokens per second per GPU at 4,096 tokens per rank. The release does not include a KV cache system, prefill and decode disaggregation, or load balancing across replicas.

DeepSeek is responsible for the release, and its GitHub documentation explains how the system works. The engine stacks DeepSeek kernels including FlashMLA, DeepGEMM, DeepEP, TileKernels, DeepSelect, and custom TileLang kernels. Attention uses data parallelism, while MoE layers use expert parallelism with an expert-parallel load balancer. A draft model proposes 5 tokens per step, and a Confidence Head predicts each draft token's acceptance rate, which cuts verified draft tokens by about 30 percent. On a cache hit, DeepInfer recomputes only the last 128 tokens of sliding-window attention state, which DeepSeek says nearly halves total prefill compute in decoder layers.

The release gives developers a rare look at a frontier lab's real serving stack. DeepInfer requires Linux, GCC 13.0 or higher, Python 3.12, CUDA 13 for NVIDIA, and CANN 9.2 for Ascend. Batch-invariant inference and deterministic sampling are available on NVIDIA only, and structured outputs support regex, JSON schema, and EBNF grammars. The default checkpoint, deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017, is downloaded on first run. The articles do not say what DeepSeek plans to release next.

stories.Headline: Anthropic's safety bill would let the US block an AI model if there's imminent risk of 50-plus deaths
stories.Summary:
Anthropic has quietly pitched a draft federal AI safety bill to lawmakers on Capitol Hill, according to three people with knowledge of the efforts. The confidential draft was obtained by POLITICO and reported on October 19, 2026. It would let the government block a model's release or use only if it poses a foreseeable, imminent risk of more than $1 billion in damages, or of killing or seriously injuring more than 50 people. The risk must stem from the creation or release of a biological weapon, the model evading its developer's controls, or a cyberattack. The language mirrors that found in California's AI laws including SB 53, which was signed into law last year.

The draft, last edited September 29, 2026, would make the Department of Commerce the regulator of the most powerful AI models in the United States. It defines a frontier model as one trained using more than 10^25 integer or floating-point operations, which is ten times lower than the 10^26 threshold in California's SB 53 and Connecticut's SB 5. Large frontier developers would be those with more than $500,000,000 in gross revenue attributable to AI products and services in the preceding calendar year, or that spent more than $1,000,000,000 on development. Independent evaluators registered with Commerce would assess frontier models every 180 days, and they may be paid by the lab itself so long as payment is not contingent on results.

If evaluators find an "imminent enumerated risk," they must report it to Commerce within 72 hours, and a federal judge for the District Court for the District of Columbia could suspend a model for an initial 45 days. An Anthropic spokesperson said the bill represents proposals outlined in the company's Advanced AI Framework, which it has advocated for with federal and state lawmakers since June. The spokesperson called them sensible policies Congress should act on. The bill would also preempt some state AI laws related to public disclosure of risk, third-party evaluation, and reporting of critical incidents, while keeping state laws on children, privacy, consumer protection, and how companies use AI.

It would require frontier labs to create safety frameworks, publish transparency reports, implement whistleblower protections, and report critical safety incidents to Commerce. Capitol Hill has seen a flurry of activity on AI safety legislation this summer. In the House, Reps. Lori Trahan and Jay Obernolte spearheaded the FRONTIER Act, which would give the government the ability to stop deployment of risky models and preempt some state AI laws.

In the Senate, Majority Leader John Thune and Sens. Amy Klobuchar and Ted Cruz have been negotiating an AI safety bill intended to mitigate catastrophic risks. That effort has faced headwinds from some safety-minded groups and Sen. Maria Cantwell, who want the government to have a larger role in reviewing AI models. Other progressives, including Rep. Greg Casar and Sen. Bernie Sanders, have called for a pause in advanced AI development and a ban on superintelligence.

stories.Headline: US orders federal agencies to remove China’s DeepSeek AI from their systems
stories.Summary:
The U.S. government has ordered federal civilian agencies to stop purchasing and remove artificial intelligence products and services developed by Chinese AI startup DeepSeek from their IT systems. The Department of Homeland Security made the order public on October 19 through a Federal Register notice scheduled for publication on October 20. The restrictions had already taken effect in late July, after DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin signed the order on July 24 under the Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act of 2018. The order covers products and services developed by Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Co., Ltd., its affiliates, and third-party offerings built using DeepSeek implementations.

The supply chain security order gave agencies 60 days to remove covered technology and prohibits future purchases. It applies to federal civilian executive branch agencies but excludes the Department of Defense, the intelligence community, and national security systems. DHS cited DeepSeek's collection and storage of user data in China, the transmission of user prompts and AI-generated responses to servers in China, and security and privacy vulnerabilities identified through forensic analyses. The department warned that DeepSeek's models "present multiple threat vectors" and that use of the tools could result in the transfer of sensitive data to China if used by US government employees or vendors. Agencies can request exceptions, and during removal DHS advised monitoring network traffic, increasing logging, and implementing data loss prevention controls.

DHS said DeepSeek presents multiple threat vectors that pose significant risk to the cybersecurity of U.S. government systems. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency will oversee implementation through its FASCSA Order Implementation Team. In Beijing, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said China will resolutely safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese companies. She said China consistently opposes the overstretching of the concept of national security and the politicizing of science, technology, economic and trade issues. DeepSeek did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The move comes amid intensifying AI competition between the US and China. DeepSeek shook up the industry in January 2025 with a low-cost, high-performance chatbot, and released a new model, V4, in April. A law passed in December 2025 targeted DeepSeek's use in intelligence national security systems. The U.S. has accused DeepSeek and five other Chinese AI companies, including Alibaba and Moonshot AI, of using large-scale model distillation to extract information from American AI systems. U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping are set to meet in mid-November on the sidelines of the APEC leaders' summit in Shenzhen, China, where AI is expected to be on the agenda.

stories.Headline: INEC, others seek safeguards against AI threats to 2027 elections
stories.Summary:
Participants at the AI and Democracy Forum 2026, organised by Yiaga Africa and partners in Abuja from 14 to 16 October, warned that deepfakes, cloned voices and coordinated disinformation could undermine Nigeria’s 2027 general elections. The forum brought together the Independent National Electoral Commission, the Centre for Journalism Innovation and Development, and Dataphyte Foundation, with support from Luminate, Microsoft, Google, TikTok, the MacArthur Foundation, the International Foundation for Electoral Systems, and the German Agency for International Cooperation. Participants identified AI-generated electoral announcements, fabricated political content and targeted manipulation as threats to informed voter participation. They also warned that genuine evidence could be dismissed as synthetic, complicating efforts to establish the truth.

The forum called for human verification and compliance with legally prescribed procedures, stressing that AI-generated alerts about duplicate registrations or anomalous results should trigger human review rather than automatic deletion or rejection. It urged INEC to publish its AI governance framework and a transparent protocol explaining how physical result sheets would be captured, electronically processed, verified and collated, including how discrepancies would be resolved. The forum also recommended independent pre-election audits of electoral technology, transparent procurement and clear accountability for technology vendors. Technology platforms were urged to label AI-generated political content, improve political advertising transparency, strengthen moderation in Nigerian languages and respond quickly to deceptive impersonation.

INEC Chairman Joash Amupitan said algorithms must not determine the outcome of the 2027 elections, insisting that AI should support rather than replace human decision-making. According to the outcome document, INEC committed to finalising an AI governance framework, adopting a binding human oversight principle and deploying AI-powered cybersecurity measures against attacks on its systems. The commission also proposed an Electoral Information Integrity Coalition involving media organisations, editors, fact-checkers, civil society groups and telecommunications operators to strengthen responses to election-related disinformation. Microsoft committed to uploading INEC’s final list of candidates for the 2027 elections into its systems and databases to help restrict the generation of misleading synthetic images of candidates.

The forum identified potential benefits of AI in election logistics, voter information, cybersecurity, accessibility and the detection of duplicate voter registrations and unusual result patterns. However, it cautioned that errors in biometric matching or the extraction of figures from result sheets could affect voting rights, undermine the credibility of results and erode public trust. The forum called on political parties and candidates to adopt an ethical AI code of conduct, while urging newsrooms to establish digital forensics desks and expand public education on identifying manipulated content. At the regional level, the Economic Community of West African States and its Network of Electoral Commissions committed to finalising unified guidelines for the responsible use of AI in West African elections. The forum concluded that institutional preparedness, transparent systems, competent election officials and effective oversight would be crucial to ensuring that AI strengthens rather than undermines Nigeria’s 2027 elections.

stories.Headline: AI startup ASI valued at $3 billion in latest funding round
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence startup ASI said on Tuesday it had raised $325 million in a funding round valuing the company at $3 billion. The Series C round was led by Spark Capital, with participation from affiliates of Citadel Securities, Meritech Capital and Craft Ventures, among others. The Boston-based company develops simulation and monitoring software that helps operators forecast disruptions hours, days or weeks in advance across complex systems such as air traffic, power grids and military operations. The funding comes amid growing investor appetite for AI software used in real-world applications.

ASI said it would use the proceeds to expand deployments in energy, logistics and military environments and add to its research and engineering teams in Boston. The company secured a five-year, $99 million US Army contract in October and a 12-year, $875 million Federal Aviation Administration contract in June, covering military command systems and air traffic management, respectively. Phillip Buckendorf, founder and CEO of ASI, said that while the broader tech ecosystem spent hundreds of billions teaching AI to manipulate words and generate text, ASI is deeply focused on AI systems that can manage and control physical assets. The company did not provide further details about the new funding beyond the amount and the investors involved.

The funding round reflects continued investor interest in AI companies that apply the technology to physical infrastructure and operations rather than language models. ASI's existing government contracts with the US Army and the Federal Aviation Administration suggest that its software is already in use in critical systems. The company has not said when the new deployments in energy, logistics and military environments will begin or how many people it plans to hire in Boston. No further announcements about future funding rounds or product releases were included in the articles.

stories.Summary:
On Tuesday, October 20, 2026, U.S. stocks rose as several large companies reported stronger profits than analysts expected. Equifax climbed 10.3 percent, Hasbro rose 7.5 percent, and 3M gained 6.6 percent after each delivered better results for the latest quarter. The S&P 500 added 0.4 percent, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 524 points, or 1 percent, as of 12:41 p.m. Eastern time. The Nasdaq composite rose a more modest 0.2 percent because artificial intelligence stocks kept swinging.

Brent crude oil fell 0.8 percent to $108.69 a barrel after nearing $112 earlier in the morning, which was close to its highest price since the war with Iran began in late February. Brent has been moving between $97 and $112 per barrel this month. American Airlines rose 4.8 percent and United Airlines rose 3 percent as fuel costs eased. Braze soared 51.6 percent to $45.32 after Salesforce said it would buy the company for $47.50 per share in cash, while Salesforce fell 1.4 percent. General Motors sank 8.3 percent even though it reported a bigger profit than expected, and it announced a plan to send up to $20 billion to investors through stock buybacks.

AI stocks remained unsettled because investors worry that high interest rates will slow the borrowing that has funded purchases of AI chips. CoreWeave fell more than 6 percent early Tuesday, then swung to a 5 percent gain before settling at a 3 percent rise. A day earlier it moved between a 7 percent gain and a 3.5 percent loss after falling roughly 25 percent last week. In Seoul, the South Korean AI company Elice dropped 32 percent on its first day of trading, and the Kospi index fell 3.7 percent.

Last week was the U.S. stock market's worst since June because of weakness in AI-related companies. In Europe, the CAC 40 in Paris slipped 0.4 percent and the FTSE 100 in London fell 0.3 percent, paring larger losses from earlier in the day. A day earlier, European indexes fell sharply after violent protests raised the possibility that governments would increase spending to ease voter anger. That could put more pressure on bond markets already strained by heavy debt loads and budget worries. The articles did not say what will happen next.
