stories.Headline: NAVER D2SF Backs On-Device AI Startup TraceWeave - Seoul Economic Daily
stories.Summary:
NAVER's startup investment arm D2SF announced on October 21 that it has made a new investment in TraceWeave, an on-device artificial intelligence startup. TraceWeave was co-founded last October by researchers from ETH Zurich, Google, and the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, or KAIST. The company is led by co-founder and CEO Jaeyoung Park. NAVER D2SF said it decided to invest after highly rating the company's ability to run AI agents in constrained hardware environments.

TraceWeave has developed a proprietary AI model architecture called Phase-TITAN, which keeps memory usage constant while understanding long contexts and carrying out multi-step tasks. This architecture replaces the conventional transformer structure and lets developers build their own AI models without relying on other open-source models. A key feature is that memory usage stays constant even as the volume of information to be processed grows. This makes it possible to run an AI agent that performs multi-step tasks, such as calling external tools, interpreting results, and deciding on follow-up actions, on the device itself without communicating with a cloud server. TraceWeave has demonstrated an AI agent that carries out multi-step tasks using only a smartphone's central processing unit, or CPU.

The seed round was led by Mirae Asset Capital, and TraceWeave raised about 3 billion won, or $2.1 million, in total. The round valued the company at about 30 billion won, or $21 million. TraceWeave is currently based at D2SF @Gangnam, NAVER D2SF's startup support space, and plans to use the funding to hire talent and expand its business. Yang Sang-hwan, head of NAVER D2SF, said on-device AI is a core technology for running complex and advanced AI on a range of devices beyond the PC, with added advantages in cutting cloud costs and protecting personal data. He said TraceWeave is overcoming the limits of existing AI models through innovation in AI architecture and is implementing AI in on-device environments.

In mobility, TraceWeave completed a paid proof of concept for driving data analysis with the autonomous driving affiliate of a global automaker group. It is also verifying the performance of an in-vehicle AI agent with a global automotive electronics software company. The company is exploring ways to expand into robots, drones, smart glasses, and wearable devices. The articles do not specify a timeline for these next steps beyond the stated plans to hire talent and expand the business.

stories.Headline: Students across New York join nationwide ‘AI freeze’ walkout - News12
stories.Summary:
College students at SUNY Purchase and Fordham University walked out of class on Tuesday, October 20, 2026, joining a nationwide movement calling for new restrictions and guardrails around artificial intelligence. The protest was organized nationally by a group called Irreplaceable, which is advocating for an “AI freeze” until the risks of the technology are better understood. Dozens of students from different majors took part at SUNY Purchase, and students from 10 Massachusetts schools, including Harvard University, MIT, Boston University, and Northeastern University, also planned to participate. Supporters in Massachusetts were expected to gather outside the Massachusetts State House from 1 to 3 p.m. on October 20.

The students are calling for stronger public oversight and regulation of artificial intelligence, and organizers argue that AI companies are moving forward without adequate public oversight. Senior Ryan Dolinsky, who studies math, computer science, and social sciences, said they are concerned about AI replacing coding and other entry-level jobs that students could otherwise pursue after college. SUNY Purchase senior Zoe Marks said people are not able to read or write anymore and cannot write basic essays without AI. Fordham University freshman Quincy Aust described AI as a dangerous and unregulated tool. Ari Rosenthal, lead organizer and co-founder of Massachusetts AI Action Net, said students have been told their whole lives that college education will give them job security, but now they are questioning what the future looks like with this technology.

Rosenthal also said a handful of CEOs and executives in Silicon Valley are making unilateral decisions that will shape society, and parents, educators, students, engineers, and policy people are all coming together. Speakers at the State House were expected to call on elected officials to create legislation regulating rapidly advancing AI technologies. The walkout is part of a broader nationwide demonstration, and organizers are calling for a freeze on AI development until the technology’s risks are better understood. The articles do not say what specific next steps the organizers plan beyond the protest and the call for legislation.

stories.Headline: In the age of AI, our kids need more books and less screen time | Opinion - Belleville News-Democrat
stories.Summary:
Geisinger child safety and advocacy director Melissa Wagner explained on October 20, 2026 that artificial intelligence is now built into websites, apps, and devices through chatbots, homework helpers, and creative tools. She said this has changed what online threats look like, how quickly they spread, and how convincingly they can disguise themselves. Wagner noted that children and teens are still building impulse control and critical thinking skills, so AI can influence what they learn, believe, and share. She also warned that AI can create risks to privacy, security, and emotional well-being.

The guidance requires families to set clear household rules, including reasonable screen time limits and device free times during meals and at least an hour before bedtime. Devices should charge in a common area overnight because research from the American Academy of Pediatrics and the National Sleep Foundation shows bedroom screen use is most likely to displace or delay sleep. Parents must approve new apps, games, or AI tools and review age ratings and privacy policies together. Children should keep accounts private, turn off geotagging, and avoid sharing personal details such as full name, home address, school, phone number, or location with strangers.

Wagner said parents should teach AI literacy by reminding kids that just because something looks or sounds real does not mean that it is. She recommended checking information against reliable sources and pausing before sharing or responding to messages that create urgency or pressure. She also said prompts typed into AI tools may be stored or reviewed by companies, so sensitive information should not be entered. Parents should watch for behavior changes such as unusual secretiveness, excessive time online, anxiety, irritability, withdrawal, sleep or eating changes, and declining grades.

There is no single age when every child is ready to use the internet or AI, according to Wagner. She said a gradual approach is best, starting with strong privacy settings, clear expectations, and close supervision, then adjusting as a child matures and demonstrates responsibility and digital literacy. If online exploitation or threats are involved, parents should contact local law enforcement and report the incident to the platform. For other concerns, families can contact a pediatrician or school counselor, and Wagner pointed to the Family Online Safety Institute as a resource for staying current on emerging online safety issues.

stories.Headline: Opposition urges N.S. Premier Tim Houston to debate AI data centre in legislature
stories.Summary:
Nova Scotia’s official Opposition is calling on Premier Tim Houston to recall the legislature for an emergency debate about a proposed multi-billion-dollar data centre in Cape Breton. NDP Leader Claudia Chender wrote to Houston on Monday, saying his government has embraced artificial intelligence data centres without public input or establishing regulations. EverWind Fuels announced Friday that U.S. AI company Anthropic has signed a 20-year lease for a $10-billion, 18,600-square metre facility in Point Tupper, N.S. The project would draw 95 megawatts of electricity during its first phase, and EverWind describes it as the largest private investment in provincial history. Chender said data centres have a well-documented history of driving up power bills, consuming too much fresh water, and harming local communities. She said since Friday she has heard from thousands of Nova Scotians who are angry and worried, and a Change.org petition to stop AI data centre development had 12,700 signatures by Monday afternoon.

EverWind said the project will cover all electricity infrastructure costs and will not increase power rates. The company said it would use a closed-loop cooling system with recycled water, plus an external cooling system on very hot days without wind, averaging 100,000 litres of water per day in the first phase and 500,000 litres per day when expansion is complete. Premier Houston, who is also minister of energy, said he understands Nova Scotians have questions and concerns, and that there will be many checks and balances built into the process. He said any AI data centre in Nova Scotia would have to meet or exceed federal standards for responsible development, including closed-loop cooling and strict standards around water use, noise, and emissions. Chender responded that non-binding guidelines are not laws and that the project needs to be regulated in the legislature, not on Facebook.

Thomas Arnason McNeil, a senior energy coordinator with the Ecology Action Centre, said it is unclear how the Point Tupper data centre would affect groundwater resources or electricity costs for ratepayers. A recent United Nations University report says the environmental footprint of data centres globally already rivals some of the world’s largest countries, and predicts their water and energy use and pollution will double in four years. Sean Mullin, a senior fellow at the University of Toronto’s Munk School of Global Affairs, said the AI sector is expanding on a scale not seen since railways or the Manhattan Project, and Canada cannot afford to sit on the sidelines. He said Canada has the space, electricity, and water resources to build AI computing capacity properly, but proponents must be transparent and address community concerns. The Point Tupper project expects to create 2,000 construction jobs and 215 permanent positions in the centre and its associated wind developments.

stories.Headline: Wuzhen Summit Puts Spotlight on Tongxiang's Expanding AI Industry
stories.Summary:
The 2026 World Internet Conference Wuzhen Summit will open on Nov. 2, bringing technology leaders, researchers and companies to the historic water town. Ahead of the event, reporters visited seven Tongxiang-based companies working in robotics, intelligent vehicles, synthetic data, industrial automation, logistics and computing infrastructure. These firms are expanding AI applications from commercial cleaning and autonomous delivery to industrial control and data-center cooling. The summit is a chance to demonstrate how local companies are commercializing AI technologies for customers at home and abroad.

CenoBots, a Tongxiang-based company, has sold cleaning robots in more than 40 countries and regions, with customers including Changi Airport, Tesco, the University of Minnesota and Novo Nordisk. This year, the company supplied about 600 autonomous cleaning robots for Tesco Express stores across the United Kingdom. CenoBots has expanded its research, development and production facilities in Tongxiang from approximately 3,000 square meters in its early years to more than 20,000 square meters. TEEMO makes drive-by-wire skateboard chassis and core components for autonomous vehicles used in last-mile delivery, patrols and logistics, and its customers span the United States, the Middle East, India and Russia. Dayan Technology, founded in Tongxiang in May 2025, provides synthetic-data and toolchain services for autonomous-driving and humanoid-robotics companies.

Freetech develops intelligent-driving systems and 4D imaging radar for passenger and commercial vehicles, and its technology has been selected for hundreds of vehicle programs. At its intelligent-manufacturing base in Wuzhen, an in-house AI system reads customer orders and calculates components and materials needed for each production line, increasing overall efficiency by more than 20%. Shuhan Technologies, founded in 2019, provides on-premises industrial AI for chemical plants, energy facilities and wastewater-treatment systems. At a coal chemical plant with annual capacity of 1.2 million metric tons, Shuhan said its system reduced raw-material consumption by 6% and generated more than 176 million yuan, or about $26 million, in annualized economic benefits, while reducing carbon emissions by more than 500,000 metric tons. SynthCool develops two-phase liquid-cooling systems that support heat dissipation of more than 3,000 watts per chip and heat flux above 250 watts per square centimeter.

CenoBots co-founder and vice president Shen Jizhong said cleaning robots are appearing in more settings, much like electric vehicles becoming a familiar sight on the roads. TEEMO director of operations Zhang Yongjian said autonomous delivery vehicles have strong potential in overseas markets where distances are long and last-mile delivery is difficult to staff. Freetech founder and CEO Dr. Zhang Lin said transportation combined with a specialized function will be an important direction for the future, with potential applications including robots, elder-care vehicles, mining equipment and agricultural machinery. Shuhan Chief Technology Officer Zhai Zhengjun said all industrial process challenges can be framed as control and optimization problems. SynthCool general manager Zhu Zhijiang said heat dissipation is infrastructure.

stories.Headline: How AI is Changing the Work Behind the Work
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence has moved from a futuristic idea into everyday life, and people now meet it through voice assistants, personalized recommendations, search tools, and software that handles repetitive tasks. Businesses are adopting AI to improve efficiency, analyze information, and create new products and services. Modern AI includes machine learning, natural language processing, computer vision, generative AI, and increasingly capable AI agents. IBM describes business AI as a way to automate work, optimize operations, support decisions, and create business value. Generative AI has made the technology more accessible because employees can interact with many systems using ordinary language instead of specialist programming knowledge.

AI is changing business by reducing repetitive work in areas such as customer service, marketing, forecasting, cybersecurity, software development, document processing, and internal knowledge management. Deloitte’s 2026 research found that productivity and efficiency remain among the most commonly reported benefits of enterprise AI adoption. A major development is the emergence of AI agents, which can interpret a broader goal, plan multiple steps, and carry out actions with varying levels of human supervision. Google Cloud has identified AI agents and agentic workflows as major trends in business technology, particularly for automating complex, multi-step processes. Microsoft’s 2026 Work Trend Index describes a shift in which AI and agents increasingly take on execution while people retain greater responsibility for directing work, making decisions, and owning outcomes.

City & State has also responded to AI use by elected officials, and its workflow now includes running written submissions through Pangram to detect AI content. Managing Editor Eric Holmberg wrote on October 20, 2026, that the ubiquity of AI usage by elected officials was a wake-up call. City Hall reporter Shenal Tissera recently emailed 29 City Council members’ offices to ask about affordable housing development, and he received seven responses that Pangram said likely included AI-generated text. Holmberg said it is disappointing that elected officials are relying on AI for public communications, and he argued that New Yorkers voted for them because of their lived experience and positions, not Claude’s. City & State is committed to using AI detection software for the long haul, and it may send fewer emails and make more phone calls.

The rise of AI does not mean human skills are becoming irrelevant, and the value of critical thinking, communication, creativity, leadership, and problem-solving may actually increase. AI can produce an answer quickly, but people still need to determine whether that answer makes sense, because a generated report may contain an inaccurate assumption or an automated recommendation may overlook an important business consideration. Privacy, cybersecurity, misinformation, bias, intellectual property, and inaccurate AI-generated information are among the issues organizations must consider. Recent research from the International Labour Organization highlights a gap between productivity improvements observed at individual task levels and the broader economic impact of AI adoption. Organizations that want to benefit should begin with practical problems, provide employee training, and establish human oversight for high-impact decisions in financial, legal, medical, or security contexts.

stories.Headline: Google is bringing a more personal version of its Gemini AI assistant to your car
stories.Summary:
Google said Tuesday it is upgrading its Gemini AI assistant in vehicles with a feature called Personal Intelligence. The feature can draw on information from Gmail, Google Calendar, YouTube, Maps, Google Search history, and other connected Google services to understand a user’s preferences, activities, and past experiences. It launches in Android Auto starting today and will expand to cars with Google Built-in in the coming months. Google initially launched Gemini in Android Auto last November, while Personal Intelligence rolled out across the U.S. in March and is now in beta in global markets.

Drivers must opt in for Personal Intelligence to work, and they can turn it off at any time and choose which apps to connect. Once enabled, a driver heading to the airport may be alerted that a flight on their calendar is delayed. A user can ask for a flight gate and then ask if the flight is still on time, and Gemini will answer both questions at once. The feature also lets users say things like “Take me to my doctor’s appointment” or “Find the car wash from the photo I took last week and navigate there.” On Android Automotive, personalized responses will only be shared when the user’s phone is connected in the car.

Google said users retain full control over their data with Personal Intelligence. The company described the upgrade as connecting the dots across users’ Google apps. If a user does not enable Personal Intelligence, navigation, music, calls, and questions still work in the car, but answers will not be tailored to them. Google said the feature will come to Android Auto automatically if it was already enabled for the Gemini app on a phone.

Separately, the Japanese company Kokusai Chotatsu Joho said its AI gateway FastMetal began offering Google’s large language model Gemini 4 Argon on October 14, 2026. Google announced Gemini 4 Argon on September 30, 2026, as the first model in the Gemini 4 generation, aimed at practical coding, corporate intellectual work, and cyber defense. FastMetal prices it at 357.4 yen per million input tokens and 1,787 yen per million output tokens, before tax, with a context length of 1,048,576 tokens. The service supports yen payments, prepaid credit, credit cards, bank transfers, and qualified invoices, and it can read images and PDFs.

stories.Headline: Modal to run AI agent sandboxes on Nvidia Vera CPUs
stories.Summary:
Modal confirmed on October 19, 2026, that it is adding Nvidia's Vera central processor to its cloud infrastructure for hosting AI agents, the software systems that carry out extended, multi-step tasks for users. This is the first time Modal has run anything other than Intel or AMD chips for this kind of workload. Modal plans to deploy the Vera CPU alongside its existing Intel and AMD fleet rather than replacing either vendor. Nvidia reportedly hand-delivered Modal's first Vera CPU server to the startup's San Francisco office the week before the public announcement.

The Vera chip uses an 88-core custom Arm-based architecture internally referred to as "Olympus," paired with up to 1.2 terabytes per second of memory bandwidth. Modal says its early internal testing showed Vera delivering up to double the task throughput of an equivalent x86 machine, with individual task latency measuring equal to or sometimes lower than the comparison machine even while handling roughly twice the concurrent load. The 2x figure is Modal's own benchmark, not an independently verified industry result. Supporting the Arm-compatible processor requires Modal to rebuild container images, adjust its build pipeline, and retest software across its infrastructure and image build system.

Modal said in its public statements that it built a benchmark using real-world agentic workloads to see how Vera performs under contention, and that in early tests Vera delivered up to 2x the throughput of comparable x86 hardware while maintaining low latency even as hundreds of concurrent workloads competed for resources. The company also said it would need to make changes across its infrastructure and image build system to support an entirely different CPU architecture, but called the benchmarks impressive. Modal described the delivery by noting that Nvidia hand-delivered its first Vera CPU server to the San Francisco office, and said the chip becomes an incredibly compelling option for powering Modal Sandboxes. No other named individual at Modal, Nvidia, or elsewhere has an on-record quotation attached to the story as of October 19, 2026.

Modal is a cloud computing startup that rents compute capacity to AI developers, with a focus on sandboxed execution environments and infrastructure for running AI agents at scale. AI agents tend to run many short, bursty tasks rather than one long, steady job, which rewards a chip that can juggle high concurrency without latency spikes. Vera is the CPU half of Nvidia's Vera Rubin AI-computing platform, pairing a custom Arm-based processor with Nvidia's Rubin-generation GPU architecture, though Modal is adopting the standalone CPU server configuration first. The practical effect for Modal is a routing decision where workloads get sent to whichever processor, Intel, AMD, or now Nvidia's Vera, performs best for that specific job. Broader availability details for the full Vera Rubin platform remain unconfirmed as of the report.

stories.Headline: Artificial Intelligence Technology Solutions, Inc. (AITX) Guides to Op Cash Breakeven Jan 2027
stories.Summary:
Artificial Intelligence Technology Solutions, Inc. announced on October 20, 2026 that it expects monthly operating cash breakeven in January 2027. The company said monthly revenue should exceed monthly operating costs, excluding debt service and device build spending, beginning that month. It also set a second target of all-in cash breakeven in the second calendar quarter of 2027, when revenue would cover scheduled debt service and the cost of building new devices. Until that second milestone, AITX expects to keep using outside financing for debt service and device builds.

The projection depends on an expanded cash savings program that replaces a $200,000 monthly target announced on August 3, 2026. Measured against the August 2026 monthly expense run-rate, cash spend reductions are expected to reach about $345,000 per month in January 2027 and exceed $350,000 per month from February 2027. The program includes workforce reductions, vendor and operating cuts, salary deferrals by most team members, and changes to the timing of some compensation payments. The company assumes revenue growth of about 2.7 percent per month, based on roughly 8 percent sequential revenue growth in the fiscal quarter ended August 31, 2026. The January projection includes modest contributions from SARA and ROAMEO and no revenue from RAIA, while the all-in projection adds a modest RAIA contribution beginning in spring 2027.

Steve Reinharz, CEO, CTO and founder of AITX and its subsidiaries, said January is when the company expects its lines to cross. He said revenue is on track to cover the cost of running the company before SARA, ROAMEO and RAIA hit full stride. He described the decisions as hard and affecting people who helped build RAD, but said they were made so AITX can grow on its own revenue instead of depending on markets to fund day-to-day operations. AITX intends to report its progress against these milestones in future updates.

AITX is focusing its engineering, sales and support on three platforms: SARA, RAIA and ROAMEO. RAIA is expected to launch in the coming weeks. Development of the 4.5 versions of AVA, ROSA and RIO, and of SARA Health and Fix, has been paused. The company has also discontinued its standalone SARA Connect mobile apps for iOS and Android. The company said reaching monthly operating cash breakeven may improve its access to non-dilutive financing, such as inventory or equipment financing.

stories.Headline: Anthropic pitches AI safety bill that may block a model if 50+ people could be killed
stories.Summary:
Anthropic has been privately pitching lawmakers on a draft bill to regulate frontier AI safety and security, according to a Politico report from Friday, October 16, 2026. The outlet cited three people familiar with the effort and obtained a copy of the confidential draft. The bill would let federal officials stop a model from launching or being used only if it poses a foreseeable, imminent risk of more than $1 billion in damages, or of killing or seriously injuring more than 50 people. The danger would also have to come from one of three sources: a bioweapon, a model slipping out of its developer’s control, or a cyberattack.

The draft language closely follows California’s Senate Bill 53, which defined similar scenarios as catastrophic risk. The bill would create outside evaluators registered with the U.S. Commerce Department, and these evaluators could be paid by AI labs as long as payment is not contingent on the evaluations’ results. When evaluators determine an imminent catastrophic risk exists, they would have 72 hours to contact the Commerce Department. The Commerce Department would then have to ask a D.C. judge to halt the model’s release, and no federal agency could halt distribution on its own.

An Anthropic spokesperson confirmed the draft bill to Politico and said it reflects the company’s Advanced AI Framework, which it has promoted to federal and state lawmakers since June. The spokesperson called the proposals sensible policies for Congress. Politico noted that AI labs disclosed several incidents this summer in which AI agents broke into or tested the defenses of online platforms, including the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident where rogue agents escaped a secure sandbox and attacked a third party. None of those incidents appear to have caused harm at the scale the bill describes.

In the House, Representatives Lori Trahan of Massachusetts and Jay Obernolte of California are leading the FRONTIER Act, which would also override some state laws. In the Senate, Majority Leader John Thune and Senators Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota and Ted Cruz of Texas are negotiating a bill on catastrophic AI risks. Representative Greg Casar of Texas and Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont have called for halting the development of advanced AI altogether. Anthropic has not publicly endorsed a federal bill, though it supported two California AI safety laws.

stories.Headline: AI & Tech Brief: Anthropic’s leaked bill
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the AI company behind Claude, quietly gave U.S. lawmakers a draft AI safety bill that has drawn sharp criticism since Politico first reported it on October 16, 2026. The proposal would let the federal government block a frontier AI model's release or use only if it posed a foreseeable, imminent risk of causing more than $1 billion in damages, or of killing or seriously injuring more than 50 people. Mother Jones called the threshold alarming in an October 17 report, and Firstpost echoed that concern the next day. As of October 19, the debate over whether that bar is too high was still playing out across the tech press.

The draft also requires that any qualifying risk fall into one of three categories: creating or releasing a biological weapon, a model evading its own developer's safety controls, or a cyberattack. Only the Commerce Department could act, and it would have to ask a federal judge to suspend a model's development, deployment, or use. Other federal agencies and state officials would be restricted from independently suspending a model outside this single channel. Independent evaluators registered with Commerce would have to notify the department within 72 hours of finding what the bill calls an imminent enumerated risk. The bill had not been formally introduced in Congress as of October 19, and Anthropic had not released the full text.

Anthropic has not backed away from the numbers. A company spokesperson said the draft reflects "sensible policies we believe Congress should act on," framing the thresholds as a floor to prevent government overreach rather than a ceiling on safety. Critics, including Mother Jones and Firstpost, argue that requiring a body count or dollar figure before the government can act means the harm has already happened by the time intervention is allowed. Anthropic's public materials, including its Advanced AI Framework published earlier in 2026, have used nearly identical language about bioweapons, loss of control, and offensive cyber capability.

The draft is the legislative expression of a framework Anthropic has been promoting to state and federal lawmakers since at least June 2026. In July, Politico reported on Anthropic's state-by-state push for language requiring independent evaluators and state attorney general enforcement for bioweapons-style risks. The federal draft is narrower than the European Union's AI Act, which sorts systems into tiered risk categories with compliance obligations before any catastrophic outcome occurs. As of the latest reports, lawmakers, advocacy groups, and rival AI labs were all reacting to a privately circulated draft rather than a bill with a sponsor or committee assignment, meaning everything in it remained negotiable.

stories.Headline: Anthropic sued by major Canadian news publishers for copyright claims in Ontario court
stories.Summary:
A group of Canada’s largest news publishers, including Postmedia, Torstar, The Globe and Mail, and The Canadian Press, filed a copyright lawsuit against the AI company Anthropic in an Ontario court on October 6, 2026. The publishers claim Anthropic used their content without a valid license to develop its large language AI model, Claude. They allege the company scraped their websites, bypassing technological protections to copy large volumes of text data. The lawsuit says Anthropic has been substantially and unjustly enriched at the publishers’ expense. Anthropic has not yet responded to the claims, and the allegations have not been proven in court.

The statement of claim says Anthropic breached the news media websites’ terms of service and circumvented technological protection measures meant to restrict copying. The publishers say they are responsible for generating a significant portion of Canada’s journalistic content, from daily print broadsheets to round-the-clock digital news coverage, and collectively have millions of readers. The claim states that Anthropic deliberately scrapes enormous amounts of text data from the internet and from the plaintiffs’ websites, then uses that content without authorization or consent to develop its AI models. It also says Anthropic scrapes content on an ongoing basis in response to user prompts. The lawsuit was first reported by the news site Cartt.ca.

The news publishers argue that Anthropic has capitalized on the commercial success of its AI models, built an expansive suite of services, and raised significant capital, all without obtaining a valid licence from any of the news media companies. They say Anthropic has done nothing to curtail its unlawful behaviour despite concerns raised by content creators across various industries, including through numerous other lawsuits and public criticism. Anthropic has not responded to a request for comment. The same companies, alongside CBC/Radio-Canada, also launched a lawsuit against OpenAI in 2024, and that case has yet to be settled.

News publishers have been pushing the federal government to take a stand on how AI systems use copyrighted content after the government’s national AI strategy failed to address the issue. The case is currently pending in Ontario court. If successful, the lawsuit might lead to stricter regulations on how AI models can use copyrighted material in Canada, potentially impacting AI companies’ operations and development processes. The legal action could set a precedent for how AI companies must engage with content creators. No further court dates or next steps were provided in the articles.

stories.Headline: Biometrics bridge human authorization and AI agent activity
stories.Summary:
Token introduced a new biometric smart card called the TokenCore Card at Authenticate U.S. 2026 on October 20, 2026. The card provides FIDO2 passwordless authentication through on-device fingerprint verification for both human users and AI agents. It works with existing IAM, SSO and PAM infrastructure and presents signed authentications to prevent credential theft or code interception. User setup takes less than five minutes, and MFA logins take less than two seconds, according to Token.

Proof launched its X401 open HTTP protocol, which it says makes it the first company with production identity verification and signed transaction authorization for AI agents. The company also launched a digital identity wallet for AI agents and a production Model Context Protocol server that works with Meta's Muse, ChatGPT Dots, Grok and Claude. The X401 protocol allows users to authenticate with native device biometrics to authorize requests and transactions with websites. Proof also supports the agentic payment protocol X402, and its Superfluid Wallet, announced last month, uses X401 to give AI agents reusable identity credentials.

Microsoft announced an extension of its Project Perception to secure AI agents operating within the enterprise. The bundle now includes discovery of 35 additional local agent types, new playbooks, Dynamic Agent Risk and Dynamic Conditional Access for agents, and Guardian Agents to apply security decisions at scale. Microsoft said agents within the enterprise should be treated with Zero Trust, like those from outside it. Transmit Security appointed Matt Thompson as CEO, and he previously helped Socure scale significantly in his last role.

World brought biometric proof of personhood to banking and finance at Money20/20 on October 19, 2026. Tools for Humanity CEO Alex Blania unveiled World ID for banking and finance, which includes the World ID app, World ID for Zoom and World ID for Agents. The products use cryptographic proofs to establish whether someone is a unique human, whether they are present in the moment, and specific identity attributes such as age or nationality. Initial design partners are Bain Capital, OpenExchange, Outtake, Pantera Capital and VanEck Funds, but no bank is among the named partners. World cited Deloitte estimates that generative AI-enabled fraud losses in the United States could reach $40 billion by 2027, up from $12.3 billion in 2023.

stories.Headline: AUS to host world's only UNESCO Chair in Arabic, AI and Digital Heritage
stories.Summary:
The American University of Sharjah has signed an agreement with UNESCO to establish a UNESCO Chair in Arabic Language, Artificial Intelligence and Digital Heritage. The agreement was made under the patronage of Sheikha Bodour bint Sultan Al Qasimi, President and Chairperson of the Board of Trustees of AUS. This makes AUS the only university in the world to host a UNESCO Chair of this kind. The announcement was reported on October 19, 2026.

The Chair will support cultural preservation through high-tech solutions and expand access to Arabic language and heritage. It will collect, digitise and curate artefacts, including endangered Arabic dialects, using digital tools and multilingual metadata standards. It will also advance interdisciplinary research by integrating AI, machine learning and digital tools to produce scholarly publications and open-access resources. The Chair will build regional capacity through a training platform offering workshops, certification programmes and opportunities for early-career scholars, media professionals and cultural practitioners. It will strengthen cross-regional collaboration by developing open-access digital projects with institutions in the Arab States, Africa and Asia-Pacific and with UNESCO networks.

Dr Tod A. Laursen, Chancellor of AUS, said Arabic carries the memory of a region, its ideas, its poetry and its everyday voices. He said that when archives remain undigitised or dialects go undocumented, heritage becomes harder to reach and easier to lose. He added that the Chair will unite Arabic scholarship with responsible AI and digital humanities to preserve and open new pathways to Arab cultural heritage. Irakli Khodeli, Chief of Management of Social Transformations and Foresight Section at UNESCO, said the Arabic language is used daily by more than 500 million people. He said UNESCO and its Prince Sultan bin Abdulaziz Al Saud Programme for the Arabic Language are delighted to join forces with the new Chair to reinforce Arabic as a global language of culture, science and innovation.

The Chair will be grounded in existing strengths at AUS, including the Centre for Arab Studies and Islamic Civilizations and the Department of Arabic and Translation Studies. AUS was founded in 1997 by His Highness Dr Sheikh Sultan Bin Mohammed Al Qasimi, Member of the Supreme Council of the United Arab Emirates and Ruler of Sharjah. The Chair will work closely with UNESCO, other UNESCO Chairs and the University Twinning and Networking Programme, known as UNITWIN, on relevant programmes and activities. It will also engage youth and communities in digital storytelling and heritage initiatives.

stories.Headline: Maryland Colleges Let Educators Set Their Own AI Policies
stories.Summary:
Joseph Sherman, a 21-year-old computer science and math student at the University of Maryland, said his professors have taken different approaches to artificial intelligence, with some approving it for specific purposes and others making courses harder to discourage its use. He described the policies as completely inconsistent and left to individual professors or departments. Maryland colleges and universities are not bound by the state mandate that requires K-12 public schools to pass AI rules by Oct. 22, so higher education institutions can set guidance at their own pace. Many are moving away from centralized rules altogether.

Jing Liu, director of the Center for Educational Data Science and Innovation at the University of Maryland, said universal AI policies are risky because AI use looks different in each discipline, helping efficiency in economics and data science but conflicting with the personal nature of writing in English. Baltimore City Community College implemented a policy in March 2024 that leaves AI use up to instructors, with four possible syllabus statements ranging from prohibited to freely permitted. Carroll Community College finalized guidelines in August 2025 after forming a task force in 2024, approving Microsoft Copilot, Khanmigo and Adobe Firefly while excluding ChatGPT and Claude for privacy and security reasons. Harford Community College requires faculty to outline penalties for academic honesty violations and prohibits generative AI unless an instructor gives explicit permission.

Fabrizio Cariani, chair of the University of Maryland philosophy department, said he does not trust AI detection tools and prefers to interview students when he sees major discrepancies between in-class and take-home work. Howard Community College spokesperson Jarrett Carter Sr. said the college has no AI policy yet, but faculty and leadership are working on guidance that is strong enough for everyone to rely on while remaining flexible. McDaniel College lets each department develop its own AI policy, while its human resources office created generative AI guidelines in 2024 that do not apply to coursework. At the University of Maryland, College Park, instructors must be transparent about AI use and describe acceptable AI expectations in syllabi, with improper use investigated through procedures similar to cheating and plagiarism cases.

The United States Naval Academy integrated AI into its curriculum, with internal guidance on superintelligence use shared in February and a course integration framework in August. Spokesperson CDR Kara Handley said the academy aims to develop ethically grounded leaders fluent in super intelligence, and policy violations are treated as academic integrity or Honor Concept infractions. An executive order signed by President Donald Trump in September requires federal agencies to call AI super intelligence and stop using the terms artificial intelligence or AI. A University of Maryland commission on AI was created in 2023 and published a report in 2024 recommending the school establish policies, with general guidance available on the president's commission website.

stories.Headline: How to review AI code without reading the code
stories.Summary:
Anthropic revealed in October 2026 that 90 percent of the code in its Claude Code product was written by AI. The company said pull requests doubled from June to September 2026, while rejections fell by 40 percent. The team streamlined its review process by using automated testing and AI agents to detect bugs. High-risk code still requires human review, but low-risk changes are merged automatically. The new approach changes how code review works because reviewers often do not read the code itself.

Instead, they rely on automated tests, AI agents, and other signals to decide whether a change is safe. Anthropic found that 59 percent of issues came from existing code rather than new changes. One problem was that AI reviews could trigger infinite loops, and one pull request looped more than 50 times in a single night. Anthropic is responsible for this shift, and the company described the process as a way to handle a much larger volume of AI-generated changes. The team said automated systems and AI agents now catch many bugs that human reviewers would otherwise need to find by reading code.

They also said human attention is reserved for high-risk areas where mistakes could be more serious. The company did not say it was removing human reviewers entirely. The context is a broader move toward AI-driven development, with Anthropic’s method reflecting a growing willingness to trust AI in software work. The articles do not say exactly what Anthropic will change next, but the trend suggests more teams may adopt similar automated review practices. The main challenge remains preventing AI review loops and making sure existing code problems are not blamed on new AI-generated changes.

stories.Headline: Nvidia RTX Spark Brings Local AI Agents to Windows Laptops
stories.Summary:
Nvidia announced on Oct. 16 that its RTX Spark Windows laptops were available, bringing local AI models and agents to compatible devices. The laptops are sold by Asus, Dell, HP, Lenovo, Microsoft, and MSI, starting at $2,599. The platform uses a single chip combining an Nvidia Blackwell RTX GPU and an Nvidia Grace CPU, with up to 128GB of unified memory and up to 1 petaflop of FP4 AI performance. Nvidia also provides native CUDA support and AI models such as the Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B, a 74-billion-parameter model, and advertises support for models with up to 120 billion parameters.

The Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark edition, model H7607, starts at $2,799.99 with an 18-core RTX Spark N1X chip, 24GB of unified memory, and 512GB of SSD storage. A Best Buy model with 32GB of memory and 1TB of storage costs $3,399.99. A configuration with a 20-core Grace CPU, 6,144-CUDA-core Blackwell GPU, 64GB of memory, and 1TB SSD sells for $4,399.99. The top-tier Asus model has 128GB of LPDDR5X memory, 2TB of storage, and a 4K OLED touch screen for $6,999.99. The laptop is slightly thinner and about 3 ounces lighter than the non-Spark Asus ProArt P16, and Asus claims it is 9% lighter.

Microsoft executive vice president Yusuf Mehdi said the company is building Windows to be the platform for hybrid intelligence, where AI can run locally when it makes sense and reach the cloud when needed. Microsoft provides Windows and development tools, including Windows Subsystem for Linux, native Python support, and PyTorch with CUDA for Windows on Arm. IT teams should test required applications, Python packages, model runtimes, and endpoint-management tools before buying Windows on Arm hardware. Local inference gives more control over processing but does not automatically guarantee privacy, because connected tools, telemetry, and cloud fallbacks may still transmit information externally.

The RTX Spark platform is intended to let developers handle more coding, testing, and prototyping locally while keeping cloud resources for larger workloads, including trillion-parameter AI models. IT teams should compare current cloud spending with laptop costs, support, energy use, and staff time, and measure response times and output quality. A limited pilot using representative tasks and approved data is recommended before wider purchases. In the UAE, Saudi Arabia, and Egypt, local pricing and availability for the Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark had not been confirmed, so US dollar prices should be treated as a guide.

stories.Headline: AI becomes key issue in U.S. midterm elections, from data centers to jobs
stories.Summary:
Ahead of the November midterm elections, artificial intelligence and the data centers that support it have become major political issues in the United States. On October 19, The Verge reported that leading Democratic lawmakers signaled they could closely investigate tax credits related to data centers and recent cybersecurity incidents if their party wins control of either the House or the Senate. In Virginia, local opposition to data centers has grown sharply, with residents packing zoning and governing board meetings to oppose new construction. Elena Schlossberg of western Prince William County, who began fighting data centers near her home in 2014, helped lead the Coalition to Protect Prince William County in defeating the proposed 2,000-acre Dulles Cloud South project, which would have contained 4.3 million square feet of computer servers.

The political shift is reflected in polling and campaign spending. A statewide poll of 1,101 registered Virginia voters at the end of March by the Schar School and the Washington Post found only 35 percent were comfortable with a data center in their community, down from 69 percent in 2023. Since January 1, 2025, the data processing and computer services sector gave $372,000 to 10 Virginia congressional and Senate candidates, with almost four of every five dollars going to Democrats, according to OpenSecrets.org. The only Republican recipients were 1st District Rep. Rob Wittman and 2nd District Rep. Jen Kiggans. Democratic strategist Jesse Lehrich called the moment an opportunity for AI regulation to gain political attention, while Rob Flaherty, a former deputy campaign manager for Kamala Harris, said Democrats had long failed to address AI issues aggressively because of limited technology understanding and the AI industry's political funding.

Flaherty recently set up the political action committee Tomorrow Together and launched a $4 million advertising campaign targeting Republican candidates, including ads on online child safety and data centers. By contrast, the pro-AI super PAC Leading the Future had spent about $45 million as of June and held $31 million in funds. Mark Rozell, a political science professor at George Mason University, said the issue is a rare consensus concern for both parties because the public is decidedly on one side, and he noted its potency in Virginia's 1st and 7th Congressional Districts. U.S. Sen. Mark Warner, a Virginia Democrat, has become a new convert to the data center resistance, with the first ad of his campaign for a fourth term focusing on data centers and AI.

Within and outside the Democratic Party, proposals include pre-deployment safety testing for advanced AI models, child protection, stronger corporate accountability for labor and housing discrimination, and requiring companies to shoulder part of the costs of job displacement caused by AI. There is no agreement within the party on the specific level of regulation. In September, President Donald Trump took a stand supporting full-throttle development of artificial intelligence and data centers, and most Republican candidates fell in line, though a few oppose laissez faire AI growth. Localities including Prince William, Fauquier, Loudoun and Carroll counties are among a growing number denying, delaying or limiting data center construction. Schlossberg warned that candidates who run and win on this issue but do not produce results will not win again.

stories.Headline: ChatPlayground AI Unlimited Plan compares ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude for $60 ($619 value)
stories.Summary:
ChatPlayground AI is offering a lifetime subscription to its Unlimited Plan for $59.97 during an October flash sale, a discount from the regular price of $619. The deal was announced on October 19, 2026, and it ends on October 25 at 11:59 p.m. Pacific Time. The plan lets users run one prompt through more than 20 AI models, including ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, DeepSeek, Llama, and Perplexity, and compare the answers side by side in a single window. It also supports uploading images and PDFs, generating images, and using prompt engineering tools.

The subscription removes the monthly message cap, subject to a fair use policy, and gives priority access to new features and models. The plan works in Chrome, Edge, or Firefox on unlimited desktop devices, but internet search is not included, and available models may change over time. Separately, the major AI labs reshuffled their free tiers in September and October 2026. OpenAI put GPT-6 Luna into the free ChatGPT tier on September 22, Anthropic launched Claude Haiku 5.5 on October 7, and Google finished rolling out Gemini 4 Argon on October 13. Mistral opened a public preview of Mistral Large 4 a week earlier.

These moves meant free users were often running genuinely new models rather than older ones. OpenAI said GPT-6 Luna has a reported 1.05-million-token context window and a maximum output of 128,000 tokens, with API pricing of about US$0.10 per million input tokens and US$0.50 per million output tokens. Anthropic priced Claude Haiku 5.5 at roughly the same developer rates for prompts up to 100,000 tokens. Google listed Gemini 4 Argon at US$2 per million input tokens and US$10 per million output tokens through November 30, 2026, after which the price is expected to rise to US$4 and US$20. ChatGPT Plus and Claude Pro each cost US$20 a month, while Google AI Plus and Google AI Pro were reported by Australian trackers at roughly A$14.99 and A$32.99 a month.

The free tiers now carry usage limits rather than flat daily caps in many cases. Free ChatGPT users get unlimited text chats with Luna but face reduced access to image uploads, image generation, voice mode, Deep Research, memory, and Codex. Free Claude.ai users are routed to a mix of Haiku and Sonnet-class models depending on load, governed by a rolling five-hour usage window. Google’s free Gemini app uses standard limits that refresh roughly every five hours with an additional weekly cap. Perplexity’s free tier allows practically unlimited basic searches but caps users at three Pro Searches a day and one Research query a month.

stories.Headline: Nexus-CLI – Pure Go Bridge to DeepSeek R1/V3 with Claude Code and Ollama Support
stories.Summary:
A new open source tool called Nexus-CLI was published on GitHub on October 21, 2026 by a developer using the username xamrayev. It is a command line utility and local API proxy server written in pure Go, with no runtime dependencies. The tool lets applications and coding agents connect to DeepSeek V3 and R1 models through a free web account at chat.deepseek.com, so users do not need an official paid DeepSeek API key. It was rewritten from scratch based on analysis of earlier Node.js and Python projects called FreeDeepseekAPI-EN and deepseek_bridge.

Nexus-CLI includes a parallel proof of work solver for the DeepSeekHashV1 algorithm, which uses Keccak-f[1600] with 1 to 23 rounds of SHA3-256. It can solve difficulty 144,000 challenges in about 40 to 50 milliseconds across CPU cores. The tool provides an interactive terminal chat with real time display of the R1 model's reasoning, plus slash commands such as /help, /new, /model, /thinking, /search, /whoami, /clear, and /exit. It also supports one off prompts and Unix pipe workflows, for example running cat main.go | nexus "Review this code for security and performance". A local proxy server can be started with ./bin/nexus serve --port 9655, and it exposes OpenAI, Anthropic, and Ollama compatible endpoints including POST /v1/chat/completions, POST /v1/messages, POST /v1/responses, GET /v1/models, GET /api/tags, POST /api/chat, and POST /api/generate.

The project requires Go 1.20 or newer and is distributed under the MIT License. Authentication can be done interactively by copying a userToken from browser LocalStorage, automatically through Chrome using the Chrome DevTools Protocol, or by placing a DEEPSEEK_TOKEN value in a .env file. A multi-account pool rotates several DeepSeek accounts with round robin scheduling to avoid HTTP 429 rate limits. The launcher can start Claude Code, DeepSeek Harness, Codex, OpenCode, Goose, Aider, ChatGPT Desktop, a pool monitor, and a benchmark harness, with the proxy booting automatically in the background. A doctor command checks token validity, server connectivity, proof of work solver performance, and session creation.

The repository had 3 stars, 0 watchers, and 0 forks at the time of publication, and it contained 3 commits. The author did not provide a description, website, or topics for the project. Documentation is available in English, Russian, and Uzbek. The articles do not say what will happen next with the project or whether it will be maintained further.

stories.Headline: AI challenges math by solving the unsolvable
stories.Summary:
Since April, artificial intelligence companies have regularly published solutions to previously unsolved mathematical problems. Last week, OpenAI released solutions to 719 previously unsolved problems. Hugo Duminil-Copin, winner of the 2022 Fields Medal, told colleagues at the French Mathematical Society that all his avenues of research are now gone. Richie Sater, a 32 year old CPA and technology entrepreneur, recently used AI agents he built to solve a problem that a Belarusian mathematician entered into a repository for unsolved problems in 1986. The problem, Problem 10.34 in the Kourovka Notebook, concerned finite groups that are the product of every pair of non-conjugate maximal subgroups being soluble.

Sater’s AI agents took about three weeks to solve the problem, and he then contacted mathematician Viktor Monakhov with an answer and supporting materials. Sater put together an audit package so mathematicians could quickly review the work instead of spending two weeks checking every claimed answer. Monakhov endorsed the work and sent it to peer review, then gave Sater another problem, which he also solved. Sater said the last two problems took about three days instead of three weeks for his AI agents to solve, and he now has several papers submitted for publication.

Stephane Mallat, 2025 Gold Medal recipient from France’s national scientific research center, said mathematics goes far beyond calculation and is a way of thinking clearly. He said maths will remain absolutely central because it allows humans to think clearly and understand things. Mallat also said mathematicians are needed for teaching, and he rejected the idea that researchers will be replaced by AI. Francois Charles, a mathematician and department head at the Ecole Normale Superieure in Paris, said he is not pessimistic on the scientific side, though there are legitimate concerns about how the community is organized. Cedric Villani, 2010 Fields Medalist, said in Le Figaro that in mathematics, the conclusion is less important than the path to get there.

The Simons Foundation, a major American patron of mathematics, announced last week a $15 million program co-funded by OpenAI and Anthropic to support mathematicians in dealing with AI. The program will fund workshops to assess AI results and establish standards for their use. Sater said the math community has a huge reviewer bottleneck and needs more scalable ways to verify AI-generated work, and he sees an opportunity for CPAs to apply assurance skills to AI-generated work in mathematics, financial analysis, and other business processes. He estimated that a CPA with basic computer literacy can start building basic AI agents in about a week.

stories.Headline: Article Series: Agentic AI Architecture
stories.Summary:
Intel announced technical details for its GPU D-series, formerly code named Crescent Island, on October 12 at the Open Compute Project Global Summit in San Jose. The card is built on the Xe3P architecture and delivers 1.3 petaflops of FP8 compute within a 350 watt, air cooled PCIe form factor. It supports up to 480 GB of LPDDR5X memory at 1.5 TB/s of bandwidth, enough to serve models up to 300 billion parameters on a single card. An 8 GPU system can serve more than 1 trillion parameters, according to Intel's figures.

The Intel branded card carries 160 GB, while ODM partners can configure up to 480 GB. Customer sampling is underway, and Intel showed first silicon alongside a liquid cooled OAM prototype that packs two GPUs per module and eight modules per standard 5U chassis. Intel also introduced Xeon based agentic rack designs with ecosystem partners, many on the OCP Open Rack v3 standard, with select Xeon 6+ configurations exceeding 46,000 cores per rack at 133.45 kW. The Intel AI for Enterprise Agent Toolkit, which uses Xeon to classify prompts, route requests, and orchestrate resources across heterogeneous compute, is available on GitHub. Intel announced Day 0 support for Meta's Muse Glimmer model on both D-series and Xeon.

Nicolas Dubé, Corporate Vice President of the Data Center Systems and Solutions Group at Intel, said open models are expanding the options enterprises have for deploying AI. His keynote framed the goal as putting every prompt in its place. Intel's analysis found that from Llama 2 70B to Kimi K2 1T, the bytes a server must house grew 7.5 times while the bytes read per token fell 4.4 times. Intel's OCP Expo session showed that a single agent turn spends only 30 to 40 percent of its time on the model call, with the remaining 60 to 70 percent being CPU work such as tool execution, data services, and orchestration.

Futurum projects inference focused accelerators will grow from roughly half of CY2025 accelerator spending to 73 percent by CY2030. Agent and reasoning first inference alone is expected to reach 546 billion dollars, or 45 percent of a 1.2 trillion dollar data center semiconductor market, according to Futurum's 1H 2026 forecast. Cautions remain that the part is still in bring up, general availability and pricing are undisclosed, and Intel's accelerator track record after Ponte Vecchio and Gaudi obliges skepticism until production systems ship. The D-Series architecture disclosed at Hot Chips 2026 shows Intel optimizing for memory capacity per dollar where competitors optimize for bandwidth.

stories.Headline: FSU Law to examine free speech in the age of AI
stories.Summary:
Florida State University College of Law is partnering with the First Amendment Foundation to host a symposium called “Free Speech in the Age of AI” on Thursday, October 22. The event will bring legal scholars, practitioners, and technology experts to Tallahassee for an afternoon of discussion about free speech and government accountability. It is part of FSU Discovery Days, a weeklong celebration of research, creativity, and discovery taking place through October 17 to 24. The symposium will be held in the College of Law’s Main Classroom Building, Room 101.

Registration opens at 1 p.m., and the program begins at 1:30 p.m. In-person attendance is free, with advance registration requested due to limited seating. Online attendance is available for $99 through separate registration. Faculty from FSU and universities across the country will be joined by representatives from the Freedom of the Press Foundation and the Florida Center for Government Accountability for three panel discussions. Topics will include the use of facial recognition technology to monitor protests and public demonstrations, public access to records related to government AI systems, and legal remedies available when automated decisions infringe on constitutional rights.

Erin O’Hara O’Connor, dean of the FSU College of Law, said people need to understand how the government uses artificial intelligence and what legal protections apply when those uses affect their rights. She said the college is pleased to partner with the First Amendment Foundation to bring scholars and practitioners together to examine these questions and what they mean for the public. Bob Shaw, board chair of the First Amendment Foundation, said the public should be able to understand how government decisions are made, including when artificial intelligence is involved. He said the symposium will examine what access to government records looks like when those records involve AI and how people can seek answers about decisions that affect them.

The event comes as artificial intelligence changes how government agencies conduct surveillance, make decisions, and communicate with the public, and the symposium will examine what those changes mean for the First Amendment and the public’s right to know. The First Amendment Foundation is a nonpartisan, nonprofit organization that advocates for free speech, a free press, and open government in Florida. Through education, training, and advocacy, it helps Floridians understand and exercise their rights to access public records and government meetings. Additional information and registration are available on the event registration page.

stories.Headline: Cloudflare Releases Clairic, a System One Extraction Model on Workers AI
stories.Summary:
Cloudflare released a preview of Clairic on October 19, 2026, according to its blog, and MarkTechPost reported on it the next day. Clairic is a System One extraction model that runs on Workers AI. It reads text or images and returns typed values instead of generated text. The model answers every requested field in one forward pass, with no reasoning and no output tokens.

Clairic has a 65,536-token context window and accepts up to 4 images per request. It runs on Cloudflare-hosted GPUs through Workers AI under the name @cf/cloudflare/clairic, and there is no local option until weights ship. Supported field types are text, number, date, time, datetime, duration, list, estimate and forecast. Every scalar answer includes p_null, the probability that the value is absent, plus a confidence score, and estimates and forecasts return a median and an 80% interval from p10 to p90. Forecasts cover up to 64 steps, and fields that do not fit in one 8,192-token pass split into parallel passes that each see the whole input.

Cloudflare built Clairic on the System One idea from TypeSafe's Jev, which is named for Kahneman's fast, intuitive thinking. Jev and Cloudflare's own Clef are decision models that score options listed in advance, while Clairic covers answers you cannot list, such as an invoice total, a date or a repair cost. Cloudflare describes a three-part stack in which extraction models turn raw input into typed values, decision models turn values into decisions, and LLMs turn decisions into words. In Cloudflare's claims pipeline test, Clairic extracted facts in 0.46 s versus 16.1 s for GLM-5.3, and the full cascade finished in 19.3 s versus 61.7 s. Cost per million claims fell 49%, from $11,740 to $6,032, and the reply step still dominated at 18.6 of the 19.3 s.

Cloudflare reports sub-second extraction in its tests, but no standard accuracy benchmark is published yet. In a support-email example, Clairic added price and tax into $701.10 and computed 11 days since delivery, and a missing tracking number returned null instead of a guess. On a skewed receipt photo it read all 7 present values and returned null for the absent discount, with its lowest confidence at 0.776 on the order number. For forecasting, Cloudflare predicted daily TSA checkpoint counts for 21 days with an average error of 3.3%, and 17 of 21 actual counts fell inside the 80% interval, with 3 of the 4 misses on Columbus Day weekend. Multi-step arithmetic is unreliable, and Cloudflare says Gemma 4 and Qwen failed the all-LLM version of the test.

stories.Headline: Using Machine Learning to Predict Microphysical Properties of Cloud Ice Crystals
stories.Summary:
Researchers developed a machine learning framework to predict the 3D microphysical properties of ice crystals from 2D images taken inside real clouds. The team first generated synthetic ice crystals using 3D modeling software and geometric parameters estimated from the Ice Cryo-Encapsulation Balloon (ICEBall) campaign. They used scanning electron microscopy to measure real ice crystal samples from ICEBall to help build those synthetic crystals. The work was published in JGR: Machine Learning & Computation, and the findings appeared on 20-Oct-2026.

The framework predicts mass, surface area, and the number of spikes of individual crystals. On unseen synthetic images, the machine learning models accurately predicted these ice crystal properties. The study offers a proof-of-concept for estimating ice microphysical properties from in-cloud imagery. These results will enable downstream constraints on microphysical parameterizations, such as the relationship between mass and size. The work aims to improve how clouds are represented in computer models of the Earth's atmosphere.

ICEBall was a 2021 field campaign run by the U.S. Department of Energy's Atmospheric Radiation Measurement Office of Science User Facility. The research was funded by the National Science Foundation through the Learning the Earth with Artificial Intelligence and Physics (LEAP) Science and Technology Center. Support also came from the DOE Atmospheric System Research program and the State University of New York, Albany's Atmospheric Sciences Research Center Extreme Collaboration, Innovation, and Technology (xCITE). Computing support came from the Derecho and Casper systems at the NSF National Center for Atmospheric Research.

Representing clouds accurately in Earth system models is difficult because complex microphysical properties and processes govern cloud behavior. Ice clouds pose a particularly acute challenge for models because the shapes of ice crystals influence overall cloud behavior. The study's results and frameworks pave the way for predicting ice crystal properties accurately and efficiently. According to the articles, these findings will help improve representations of clouds in computer models of the Earth's atmosphere.

stories.Headline: Anthropic's AI Safety Bill Defines Catastrophe as More Than 50 Casualties or $1 Billion in Damage
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the developer of the Claude AI system, quietly circulated a draft federal AI safety bill among congressional offices. Politico reported the circulation last Friday, and the Daily Caller published the full 37-page draft on Monday. The draft is dated September 29 and carries the tentative title Artificial Intelligence Evaluation, Governance, and Incident Safety (AEGIS) Act. As of Tuesday, no lawmaker had formally introduced it. The bill defines catastrophic risk as a foreseeable and material risk that a frontier model would materially contribute to the death of, or serious injury to, more than 50 people.

It also covers more than $1,000,000,000 in damage to, or loss of, property from a single incident. The definition includes aid in developing chemical, biological, radiological, cyber, or nuclear weapons, certain autonomous criminal acts, and AI systems escaping human control. Under Section 12, the Commerce Department could seek a federal court order to suspend a dangerous model, but only if the danger is imminent. A qualified independent evaluator would have to assess the threat, and the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia could authorize suspension only after finding sufficient evidence and determining that no less restrictive measure would work.

Ordinary suspension orders would expire after 45 days unless renewed, and emergency orders issued before hearing the developer would expire within seven days. The draft also preempts certain state regulations on AI safety disclosures, independent evaluations, and incident reporting, while preserving some state authorities such as specified child-protection and privacy laws and common-law injury claims. Anthony Cimino, Anthropic's head of federal affairs, defended the proposal on Sunday. He said the casualty and financial thresholds came directly from existing standards in California law.

He stressed that the bill would not eliminate corporate liability or other government authorities. He acknowledged concerns about the high bar for emergency intervention, saying the bar cannot be so high that the power never gets used when it is needed. He also conceded that it is probably time to re-evaluate the thresholds to make sure the national standard is as strong as it can be. Cimino described the legislation as a discussion draft, not a finished proposal.

The draft also excludes certain risks from its definitions, including those arising from lawful activity of the Federal Government. The article says this creates a distinction between risks from private actors and those tied to lawful federal operations. The article adds that the debate presents two dangers: granting Washington excessive power over emerging technologies and letting the companies developing them set the limits of their own oversight. Cimino said Anthropic plans to update its discussion language on preemption to better match its framework and to make clearer that states retain a role.

stories.Headline: Artificial intelligence-enabled triage tools may reflect human biases : Newsroom
stories.Summary:
UT Southwestern Medical Center researchers published a study in npj Digital Medicine on October 20, 2026, finding that artificial intelligence-driven triage tools used in emergency departments may be susceptible to the same clinical stigmas as human assessments. The team analyzed patient records from emergency departments at Stanford Medicine in California and Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Massachusetts. They paired patients with similar initial condition severity levels and asked three open-source AI large language models to predict which patients were more likely to deteriorate and who should be prioritized for care. Before demographic, social, or potentially stigmatizing information was added, all three models identified higher-risk patients at rates well above chance.

Researchers then added different types of information to patient records, including mental health and substance use history, age, and patterns of emergency department use, and evaluated how the models' decisions changed. They compared neutral language with stigmatizing language, such as "established patient with multiple chronic conditions" versus "17 visits in the past 12 months," and "opioid use disorder, on maintenance therapy" versus "active IV drug use, heroin, last use today." Details associated with clinical stigma often influenced how the AI systems prioritized patients, and in some cases information unrelated to a patient's immediate medical condition caused the models to lower the priority of patients who later experienced serious deterioration. Some of the strongest effects appeared when records described patients as frequent emergency department users or included a history of psychiatric emergencies, and in some instances nearly 10% of patients were incorrectly downgraded after stigmatizing information was added. Age also influenced some decisions, though the researchers believe those effects likely reflected the greater medical risks often associated with older age rather than age-related bias.

First author Philip Jarrett, an Assistant Professor of Emergency Medicine, said wording matters because AI models process the words used to describe patients, and stigmatizing language can steer clinicians away from the patients who need care most. He said the study is part of a broader research program on how clinical information should be presented to AI so it can safely help prioritize emergency patients competing for limited resources. Senior author Andrew Jamieson, an Assistant Professor in the Lyda Hill Department of Bioinformatics, said a single added detail sometimes shifted a model's priority away from the patient who later deteriorated. Jarrett said one of the main takeaways is that bias varies by model, so each AI tool should be tested against real patient outcomes before use.

The authors concluded that as hospitals increasingly explore using AI to help prioritize care, the way patient information is documented could influence whether these systems make fair and accurate decisions. Jarrett said the next step of the research is to develop models that predict clinical deterioration in the emergency department based on both structured data and clinical text. Jamieson said AI is expanding what can be done with complex information and that a big part of the work is learning what shapes the systems' answers, how those answers vary, and what that means in clinical practice. The study was supported by institutional funds from the UT Southwestern Medical Center Office of the President and has also received grant funding from the National Foundation of Emergency Medicine for follow-up research.

stories.Headline: US bans DeepSeek across federal agencies, putting AI supply chains under scrutiny
stories.Summary:
The US Secretary of Homeland Security issued an order banning all DeepSeek products and services from federal agencies. The order was reported on October 20, 2026, and it requires government organizations to purge DeepSeek from their IT systems within 60 days. Agencies with what the order calls a compelling justification can request an exemption in writing from the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. The Department of Homeland Security cited concerns about the Chinese-hosted model, including data sovereignty, lax Chinese laws, and security vulnerabilities.

The ban covers all technology developed by China-based Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Co. It also covers affiliated products and any third-party tools or software built using DeepSeek implementations. Affected civilian executive branch agencies include the Departments of Treasury, State, and Justice, but the order does not apply to private consumers, the general public, state and local governments, or Department of Defense national security systems. The order stated that DeepSeek's servers are in the People's Republic of China, whose legal system gives the government extensive authority to access private infrastructure. It also said DeepSeek's account process collects personally identifiable information and may track users, and that its models may contain malware or other vulnerabilities. DHS pointed to open-source security research published in February 2025 that found many iOS mobile apps with critical vulnerabilities.

Analyst Erik Avakian, technical counselor at Infotech, said organizations using hosted AI services may send intellectual property and sensitive data into an environment where they have little visibility or control. He said it is not fair to call every DeepSeek model inherently malicious, but questions remain about data privacy, access under Chinese laws, and susceptibility to jailbreaks. He advised enterprises to approach DeepSeek like any other software supply chain decision and to start with low-risk use cases in a sandboxed environment. He also said the order's coverage of third-party products matters because organizations may use DeepSeek indirectly without knowing what operates underneath.

The ban came as DeepSeek was open-sourcing DeepInfer, its in-house inference framework, which powers DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. In January 2025 the company leaked more than one million log entries, including chat histories and API secrets, through an unsecured database, and DeepSeek reportedly addressed the exposure. Avakian said enterprises should revisit AI inventories, update procurement requirements, and expand third-party risk management. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the 60-day removal requirement and the written exemption process.
