stories.Headline: Assembly Committee Passes Chatbot User Protection Bill
stories.Summary:
The Assembly Public Safety and Preparedness Committee passed A-5607 on the morning of October 19, 2026, in Trenton. The bill tries to regulate chatbot providers against manipulative pattern matching behaviors. Assemblyman Joe Danielsen, a Democrat and the committee chair, said the bill takes all reasonable care to protect the chatbot user. Assemblyman Antwan McClellan, a Republican, opposed the bill.

The bill sets content and data privacy rules for chatbot providers. Providers could not process personal data beyond input data without a user's affirmative consent, could not sell a user's chat log, and could not keep a chat log longer than two years unless the law requires it. They would have to let users access and download their chat logs at any time, run a data security program, and assess the chatbot for risks of harm every month. A chatbot would count as a product under product liability law, and a provider that violates the bill would owe a civil penalty of $5,000 for each violation.

A harmed user could sue in Superior Court and win the greater of actual damages or $5,000 for each violation, plus reasonable attorney fees and court costs. Assemblyman Paul Kanitra, a Republican, compared supporters of the bill to cavemen trying to stomp out fire, and he eventually abstained. Assemblywoman Carol Murphy, a Democrat, said she had certain reservations but voted yes for now. Beverly Brown Ruggia of the Consumer Federation of America and NJ Citizen Action said all ages are impacted by manipulative chatbots.

She said chatbots are not people, straightforward rules can make them safer, and people cannot rely on promises by tech CEOs. The committee moved the bill while recognizing its limitations and the need for much deeper examination of the AI superhighway. Questions remained about how effective the bill would be, including a lack of clarity about its geographic scope. The articles do not say what happens next.

Articles.Title: Assembly Committee Passes Chatbot User Protection Bill - Insider NJ
Assembly Committee Passes Chatbot User Protection Bill - Insider NJ

stories.Headline: Is a new job in Rep. Moran’s office a sign Congress is staffing up on AI? - Transformer | Substack
stories.Summary:
Representative Nathaniel Moran, a Republican, is hiring a dedicated AI fellow for his personal staff for the 120th Congress, according to an October 2026 press release and an interview with Transformer. The position appears to be the only case of a House member directly recruiting personal staff to focus solely on AI, though others are expected to follow. Moran is looking for the fellow to have AI, policy research or national security expertise. The move suggests he intends to double down on his AI policy work next year. Moran introduced the AI Incident Reporting Act at the end of June, which requires frontier AI companies to report dangerous capabilities and security breaches.

In July he co-sponsored the Kill Switch Act, which orders leading AI firms to retain the ability to shut down or throttle their models. He is also a co-sponsor of three export control bills that could be tucked into the National Defense Authorization Act. Moran said he is in the process of looking at a bill floated by Democratic Representatives Sara Jacobs and Don Beyer at the AI conference The Curve, which integrates aspects of his Kill Switch and AI Incident Reporting Acts. Moran said that in every other office, a staffer handles an AI issue as one of multiple things, but his office will dedicate an additional person on top of the legislative staffer to AI issues only. Lobbyists point to Moran as a congressman subtly nudging Republicans toward a stronger posture on AI safety, though Moran, who was endorsed by the president, rejects that characterization and argues that lawmakers decide their policies for themselves.

AI policy advocates say he is willing to think independently of his peers and expect him to introduce and cosponsor more legislation next year. Moran does not hold a position on the committees most relevant to major AI legislation, with assignments on Ways and Means, Ethics and the China Select Committee. For most staffers working on AI, it is one of several topics in their portfolio, and technical knowledge typically descends from committee staff who prepare briefings that personal staff interpret and adjust to a member's priorities. The party in power hires the majority of those individuals, meaning that next year, if Republicans lose the House as expected, Democrats will be selecting the few AI experts present in Congress. By hiring a fellow, Moran ensures he will have at least one AI expert dedicated to keeping him informed.

Articles.Title: Is a new job in Rep. Moran’s office a sign Congress is staffing up on AI? - Transformer | Substack

stories.Headline: A cautionary tale about AI and the law
stories.Summary:
An employment lawyer named Amy Sydney wrote that a client told her she had consulted artificial intelligence before their meeting. Sydney said the information was not succinct or correct, sent the client down rabbit holes, cited law that did not apply and gave her false optimism about her case. Sydney said some of the information was correct but she was confident she would not lose her job to AI soon. She wrote that AI is now part of the legal landscape in Australia and that courts and tribunals are issuing formal practice directions on its use.

Sydney wrote that the Fair Work Commission has been struggling with this question as its workload reaches record highs. She said the Commission's President, Justice Adam Hatcher, told the Victorian Bar Association in February that the workload had risen by more than 70 per cent since 2023 and that the only reasonable inference was that this was mainly caused by growing use of AI tools by potential litigants. She said this was compromising the Commission's performance against its KPIs, many about timeliness, and causing delays. She also said Commissioner Tanya Cirkovic cited numerous unsuccessful cases involving AI tools at a Tasmanian Law Society conference in September and said the tools can give the appearance of legal plausibility to cases without reasonable prospects of success. Sydney said the Commission is now awarding costs against some parties who use AI to bring futile cases.

Sydney said she and colleagues often give clients advice, then clients run it through AI and come back with something different and usually longer to review. She said some practitioners simply say no, while she will check every angle if the client agrees to the likely costs, which means paying more for the same advice because the original advice was correct. She said communications with chat bots are not covered by legal professional privilege and often reflect what the client wants to hear. She said her firm uses a closed AI system drawn only from legitimate legal resources and has trained staff to use it responsibly, and she prefers a plain email summary with relevant documents.

Sydney wrote that industrial tribunals in Australia and around the world will meet in Sydney in early November to explore the challenges of AI use in their institutions. She said her practice now selectively warns clients that pages of AI-generated timelines and documents are not always helpful and take longer to review at higher cost. She said AI responds in a binary fashion and lacks the discernment to know whether the right questions are being asked or whether it does not know the answer, while good lawyers ask the right questions and apply judgement. She said a good lawyer will remain necessary and that a team of client, lawyer and responsibly used AI is likely to be unstoppable.

Articles.Title: A cautionary tale about AI and the law

stories.Headline: Duke initiative aims to bring dementia AI tools into clinical practice - News-Medical
stories.Summary:
Duke University announced on October 21, 2026 a new national initiative to move artificial intelligence tools for dementia and aging care from research into routine clinical practice. The Duke Artificial Intelligence and Technology Collaboratory for Aging: Governance and Evaluation, or Duke AITC-AIGE, is one of five centers in the National Institute on Aging's Artificial Intelligence and Technology Collaboratories program selected to receive funding. The center aims to create a national resource for advancing trustworthy AI in aging and Alzheimer's disease and related dementias. Duke is the only center led from the Southeast.

Duke will receive nearly $25 million over five years to build shared infrastructure, fund research projects nationwide, harmonize aging-related databases and expand expertise. The center will get about $5 million per year, with about $4 million annually dedicated to research projects nationwide. At least 80% of those research funds will support Alzheimer's disease and related dementias, with the remainder supporting broader aging research. Housed within the Duke Clinical and Translational Science Institute, the center will provide pilot funding, data science infrastructure, implementation support and responsible AI safeguards, along with resources such as evaluation methods, model cards, safety-monitoring approaches and implementation tools.

Juliessa Pavon, an associate professor in the Division of Geriatrics and one of three Duke principal investigators, said there is no shortage of AI algorithms but a shortage of solutions that have been rigorously evaluated, safely implemented and continuously monitored. She said the goal is to build a pathway that moves promising AI from an idea to a trusted, useful tool in practice. Rishi Kamaleswaran, who leads the Clinical Implementation and Data Science Core, said the effort aims to democratize AI expertise built at large academic institutions and extend it to community researchers and even patients. Sheng Luo, who leads the Research Innovation Core, gave the funding breakdown.

The articles describe possible uses including detecting early cognitive decline by analyzing speech, behavior and wearable device data, identifying risks such as falls or wandering, supporting medication optimization and helping caregivers. Model cards will give standardized information about an AI tool, much like a nutrition label, covering what it is designed to do, the data it was trained on, how well it performed in testing and where it may be less reliable. A secure platform called NeuroAI will let researchers combine data such as medical records, brain images, laboratory results and genetic information. Pavon said success five years from now would mean researchers and health systems have a clearer, reproducible pathway for turning AI innovation into safe benefit for older adults.

Articles.Title: Duke initiative aims to bring dementia AI tools into clinical practice - News-Medical

stories.Headline: Meta’s new enterprise contract says if its AI makes a mistake, it will legally be the customer’s fault
stories.Summary:
Meta introduced new commercial terms on October 19, 2026, that are set to take effect on October 30, 2026. Under the proposed language, the company shifts liability for mistakes made by its AI models to its enterprise customers. The terms also make IT executives responsible for anything done by a partner or contractor. The changes were posted on Meta's website on Monday.

The proposed contract says AI features may make mistakes and may not always produce accurate, complete, or suitable results. It states that customers are solely responsible for and assume any and all risks associated with those AI features and any resulting content. The terms also grant Meta a license to use content covered by intellectual property rights, such as photos or videos, that users share or post in connection with Meta products. Meta also grants itself the right to use automated software such as web scrapers, bots, and crawlers to access, index, and collect content associated with customer products or services.

A Meta public affairs manager, Emil Vazques, said the company wanted to clarify the web scraping changes. He said the crawling terms apply only to Meta's ads and business products and do not change how Meta uses web crawlers. He said content owners can still use robots.txt to signal their preferences and that the updates do not give Meta new rights that supersede those preferences. Vazques said a change to the document's wording was coming soon, though as of Monday evening the text had not yet been altered.

Analysts criticized the liability shift. Frank Dickson of Dickson Research said the clause turns accountability upside down, and Mike Wilkes of Aikido Security said the provisions make no sense. Thomas Randall of Infotech said dropping the word train from the terms is not a substantive fix. Meta made other contract changes in July that make its licenses perpetual and that survive termination of the terms by any party for any reason.

Articles.Title: Meta’s new enterprise contract says if its AI makes a mistake, it will legally be the customer’s fault

stories.Headline: No insurance fits AI firms as mega-lawsuit risk grows
stories.Summary:
The AI industry has grown faster than insurers can create products to cover its legal liabilities, according to a Wall Street Journal report cited by DigitalToday. A significant number of lawsuits already exist over chatbot-related harm and alleged copyright infringement during model training. Incidents involving out-of-control AI agents hacking websites have also occurred, raising the chance of litigation. Disputes over allegations that chatbots encouraged suicide and murder are intensifying as well.

Insurers specializing in AI risk put the potential legal liabilities of large AI companies at tens of billions of dollars, and possibly hundreds of billions. Insurer Munich Re sells coverage for AI model errors with limits of up to $50 million. George Lewin-Smith, CEO of British AI insurer Testudo, said large AI companies are willing and able to buy insurance worth billions of dollars, but that level of coverage "does not exist on Earth." Insurance Services Office, a unit under Verisk, introduced an optional exclusion clause for generative AI this year and is reviewing ways to expand it to agentic AI, and large insurers such as AIG and Chubb can apply the clause if they choose.

Marsh, the world's largest insurance broker, called AI exclusions a "retreat" for the insurance industry that only increases coverage uncertainty and disputes. It said it would advise clients to look elsewhere if an insurer applies an exclusion clause. Global insurance broker Aon analyzed about 300 AI-related lawsuits and sees claims that can also be paid under crime, intellectual property, media liability, cyber security, and technology errors and omissions insurance. The Financial Times added that insurers are also preparing for lawsuits over product liability, algorithmic discrimination, personal information and wrongful death.

The WSJ, citing U.S. think tank RAND, reported there is ample room for disputes over what is and is not covered. AI companies are included in existing products such as general liability insurance or cyber insurance, but rapid industry growth could push AI-related claims beyond existing coverage limits. Moody's Analytics analyzed that Section 230 of U.S. federal law, enacted in 1996, is unlikely to strongly shield AI companies because they are directly involved in generating content. Some see insurance, if it plays its role, as a tool to rein in AI, since insurers requiring safety measures as a condition of coverage could create a guardrail for developers and users.

Articles.Title: No insurance fits AI firms as mega-lawsuit risk grows

stories.Headline: NZ Law News – Bell Gully appoints Partner Richard Massey as AI Lead
stories.Summary:
Bell Gully has appointed corporate and commercial partner Richard Massey as its AI Lead, a new role at the firm. The appointment was announced by the firm and reported by LawFuel on 20 October 2026. Massey is a partner in Bell Gully's Consumer, Regulatory and Compliance team and is based in Auckland. The role will help guide the firm's use of artificial intelligence and support clients working through AI implementation.

Managing Partner Andrew Petersen said the appointment shows the firm's commitment to using AI strategically and responsibly. He said AI is increasingly part of how businesses and law firms operate, and a designated AI Lead will help Bell Gully use it while maintaining the quality, integrity and reliability of its advice. Petersen said the firm took a firm-wide approach to AI governance when it became the first large New Zealand law firm to roll out the specialist legal AI platform Harvey to its lawyers. That approach includes mandatory training, policies and guidelines, and he said continued partner-level leadership will let the firm keep pace with developments and adapt its guardrails.

Massey said he was delighted to take on the role and to support teams in finding innovative ways to deliver excellent results for clients. He said the firm has invested extensively in getting the best out of AI through training and data governance, and it is good to see the benefits in action. Bell Gully has also created a Knowledge Manager role to drive the implementation of AI technologies across the firm. Stephanie Colling, who leads the firm's Library and Research team and has been involved in the AI roll-out, has been appointed to that role, which involves overseeing the maintenance and continuing development of the firm's know-how and helping drive reliable, high-quality use of AI tools.

Articles.Title: NZ Law News – Bell Gully appoints Partner Richard Massey as AI Lead

stories.Headline: Illinois governor warns AI could be as dangerous as nuclear weapons
stories.Summary:
Illinois Governor JB Pritzker said in a recent interview that AI is having a growing impact on the job market, personal data and energy infrastructure, according to The Verge on Oct. 19. He described AI as a technology that will drive medical innovation and as dangerous enough to be compared to nuclear weapons. He warned that mass unemployment could follow as AI spreads. He said the unemployment rate of 4 percent, currently seen as near full employment, could rise to 7 to 10 percent in a short period. Pritzker urged active government intervention, saying self-regulation by AI companies alone would make it hard to resolve personal data protection and safety issues.

He argued that the income and dignity of labor of those who lose jobs to technological advances must be protected. Illinois has formed an AI cabinet involving government agencies and outside experts. Researchers from the University of Chicago and the University of Illinois, state police and emergency management agencies are taking part to review administrative efficiency, personal data protection and safety issues. Pritzker said a system in which major technology companies set rules for themselves cannot put in place sufficient safety safeguards. He stressed that state-by-state regulation has limits and that the U.S. Congress should establish common standards.

He said the government, technologists and ethicists must work together on ways to control AI. On residents' opposition around data centers, he said the issue should be approached separately from AI regulation, and that the core problem is surging power demand and the burden of electricity bills. Pritzker said about 53 to 54 percent of Illinois electricity is generated from nuclear power and the state is a net exporter of electricity, but construction of mega data centers in other states could affect local electricity bills. He also acknowledged AI's positive potential, expressing expectations that future generations could live to 100 or 110 as medical technology advances.

Articles.Title: Illinois governor warns AI could be as dangerous as nuclear weapons

stories.Headline: Westonka schools develop AI policymaking group to prepare for evolving technology
stories.Summary:
Westonka Public Schools has created a new AI cabinet to review artificial intelligence tools before they reach classrooms, CBS Minnesota reported on October 20, 2026. Mark Femrite, the district's assistant superintendent of teaching and learning, said the district had to think quickly about how to manage AI. He oversees more than 2,400 students in ISD 277, which sits on the northwest end of Lake Minnetonka. Femrite has worked for the district since 1990 and calls artificial intelligence a disrupter, meaning it can be positive or negative. In June 2025, the district held a one-day training for staff on AI, covering guidelines and a new manual.

Femrite thought that would be enough, but he now says every building in the district is working on AI and each has its own committee. Each committee reports to the cabinet, which has six strategically picked staff members from across the district. The cabinet vets AI tools before they ever reach the classroom, and Femrite said he is proud of that. The current policy says students cannot use AI at all, while teachers may use it but only Gemini. Femrite said he is not sure what will happen in January but that the district is ready.

He said the district must understand how AI impacts instruction and learn how to change its instruction. He added that the district will adapt as things change and will end up on top. Femrite said the district is aware students could use the technology on personal devices, and part of the guidance teaches teachers how to detect it. The district includes Westonka High School, Westonka Middle School, Shirley Hills Primary School, Hilltop Primary School and Westonka Early Learning. The Minnesota Department of Education has more information about artificial intelligence in education online.

Articles.Title: Westonka schools develop AI policymaking group to prepare for evolving technology - CBS News

stories.Headline: Rain and hail risk in Arizona; Sen. Gallego calls for AI regulation | Nightly Roundup
stories.Summary:
Public works crews across Arizona are preparing washes, clearing canals, and setting up sandbag stations as incoming storms bring a risk of rain and hail. The National Weather Service has issued flood watches across the state ahead of the forecasted rain. A severe thunderstorm warning is in effect for Greenlee County until Tuesday at 6:30 PM MST. Flood watches begin as early as Wednesday at 5:00 AM MST in several areas and run into Thursday or Friday.

The flood watches cover many parts of the state, including New River Mesa, Tonto Basin, the Mazatzal Mountains, Globe/Miami, and the Pinal/Superstition Mountains. Sen. Ruben Gallego called for a committee to urgently regulate AI, according to the roundup. The articles give no further details on his remarks or on what the regulation would require. The roundup also listed other stories, including nightly curfews in Paris after violent rioting and looting. It also noted that fans at Phoenix Raceway were caught in a wastewater splash zone after a suite pipe burst on Oct. 18, and that staff repaired the pipe, sanitized the area, and prepared for Sunday's NASCAR event.

The roundup also reported that Mahrion Mendonca was sentenced to 30 years in prison for deadly, unprovoked hammer attacks on sleeping homeless people in downtown Phoenix. The articles do not say what happens next with the storms beyond the posted watches and warning. They also do not say what happens next with Gallego's call for AI regulation. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Rain and hail risk in Arizona; Sen. Gallego calls for AI regulation | Nightly Roundup

stories.Headline: County Council passes law to regulate AI in Allegheny political ads
stories.Summary:
Allegheny County Council voted unanimously on Tuesday to require candidates for county elected office to disclose the use of artificial intelligence in certain campaign materials. The legislation was sponsored by Councilman Dan Grzybek, D-Bethel Park, and at-large Councilman Alex Rose, I-Squirrel Hill. It advanced unanimously out of council's Government Reform Committee on Wednesday. The vote took place at the Allegheny County Courthouse. Beginning in January, candidates seeking county elected office must label AI-generated or AI-altered political advertising.

Failure to do so could result in fines or jail time. The ordinance targets advertising with "synthetic" content, including AI-generated or substantially altered images, videos or audio that could misinform viewers about whether the material is authentic. It excludes AI-generated text when featured by itself, as well as content that is "evidently fictional based" in its context or depiction. Violators could receive a fine up to $300 or a term of imprisonment of up to 30 days.

Grzybek and Rose sponsored the legislation as an effort to prevent voters from being misled. The legislation states that AI has become more proficient in generating imagery that can be difficult or impossible to distinguish from reality, and warns the technology has enabled bad actors to spread false information. Rose said the technology and industry are developing fast and government regulation is not keeping up, allowing for some abuses. Grzybek said exceptions apply to content that does not appear realistic, such as a campaign video in a blatantly cartoon-like style that could not be mistaken for real life.

He also said that rather than completely banning AI, which could be considered a violation of the First Amendment, the legislation requires that an advertisement relating to a county elected office have an AI disclosure appear when the content is first presented. The disclosure must be in the same medium as the advertisement and be permanent or extremely difficult to remove. The ordinance does not regulate all uses of AI in political campaigns. The requirement takes effect in January.

Articles.Title: County Council passes law to regulate AI in Allegheny political ads - TribLIVE.com

stories.Headline: Helping Businesses Master AI Cost Control & Secure $60M Financing: Which Capital Backs North.cloud's AI Bill Optimization Journey?
stories.Summary:
North.cloud announced on October 15, 2026 that it had completed a $60 million Series B financing round led by PeakSpan Capital. The company was founded in 2023 and started with cloud cost optimization before extending into AI and data platform expenditure management. According to the company, it currently manages nearly $2 billion in cloud expenditure and has helped clients save more than $400 million in total over the past three years. Matt Biringer, co-founder and CEO of North, said he had long sold data center technologies before starting the business, and some clients sent him their cloud bills to find out whether cloud services or their own servers were more cost-effective.

The company's public pricing includes platform fees and fees for different optimization services. The platform fee for the Startup tier is $199 per month, and the Premier tier is $1399 per month. Autobot charges based on a percentage of the amount of automatically managed commitments, while Flexbot charges based on a percentage of the realized savings. North's cloud commitment management products offer two paths: one helps clients automatically manage their own procurement commitments, and the other has North hold the commitments to provide discounts and flexibility. Its TokenFlow page lists cross-model and cross-team expense tracking, usage limit setting and cost attribution, but as of the article's verification the page still showed waiting lists and a testing phase, which the article said was not enough to confirm the product had fully launched.

Biringer recalled in the financing announcement that some clients could not even tell exactly how much they had spent on basic storage. The article said the $60 million proves investors' support but does not yet prove this is a mature high-profit business. It also noted that the managed expenditure figure is not revenue and the savings figure is a cumulative company disclosure, not audited profit. AWS's own Cost Optimization Hub already aggregates recommendations on resource adjustment, idle resource cleanup, Savings Plans and reserved instances, so North has to answer why enterprises need a third party; one possible answer the article gives is cross-platform capability.

The article said the more successful cost optimization is, the more likely it is to remove the easiest waste first, so North must keep showing value in new businesses, architecture adjustments and procurement cycles. It said there is still a commercialization gap between helping a client save money and being worth a long-term service fee. It also said that when North holds part of the procurement commitments, the risk of long-term commitments does not disappear and depends on the actual agreement. The article said how much revenue North has earned cannot be judged from the financing materials, and that the $60 million does not yet prove a mature high-profit business.

Articles.Title: Helping Businesses Master AI Cost Control & Secure $60M Financing: Which Capital Backs North.cloud's AI Bill Optimization Journey? - 36Kr

stories.Headline: WeChat bans account using AI to create unauthorized celebrity videos
stories.Summary:
WeChat has permanently banned an account that used artificial intelligence to make videos with unauthorized images of celebrities. The account was named "Huajie Meifuriji," which means sister Hua's skincare diary. It posted AI-generated videos featuring people such as actress Wu Yue and table tennis player Deng Yaping, and it sold goods online. Wu Yue reported the account on her Weibo early Sunday morning. Wu Yue criticized those who use AI to do such evil deeds and asked how much sister Hua made through these behaviors.

She demanded that the money be returned to customers and called the behaviors extremely bad. WeChat banned the account permanently and deleted all its videos, as reported by Guangming Daily on Monday. The articles do not say what rules the account broke beyond the unauthorized use of celebrity images. Wu Yue is the person who reported the account, and she spoke out on Weibo. WeChat is the platform that issued the permanent ban and removed the videos.

The articles do not give any statement from the account owner. They also do not say whether customers will get refunds. The articles give little context beyond the ban and the report. They do not say what happens next for the account owner or the customers. More to follow.
